speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the hon. the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen), I desire to bring to the notice of the right hon. the Prime Minister the reports that have appeared in the press.this morning about the strikes at Winnipeg. It is said that certain men who have been arrested are to be tried before a lay commission composed largely of officials of the Department of Immigration. I submit to the Prime Minister that such should not be the case, that these are grave charges, and that they should be tried before the best trained jurists of the land, or judges. I wish to know from the Prime Minister what method of trial is proposed.

I think the hon. gentleman (*Mr. McKenzie) is labouring under a misapprehension in regard to the matter. The Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) has telegrams this morning from Winnipeg, Which I have not seen. 1 therefore speak under reserve and subject to any mformation - which may be contained in these telegrams. There are two entirely distinct proceedings so far as my information goes. The men were arrested under the criminal law of the country, upon the charge that they had engaged in a seditious conspiracy, and they were placed under detention upon that charge. In addition to that, there was a proceeding taken under the Immigration Act for the deportation of some or all of them-I am not quite sure which. That is entirely distinct from the criminal proceeding. They, of course, could not be tried under the Immigration Act on a crirni-

nal charge; they would be tried upon such a charge under the ordinary criminal law of the country, according to the proper criminal procedure established by law. The procedure under the Immigration Act is one which was established many years ago, which has been acted upon many times in this country during the past fifteen or twenty years, and which can be carried on, as I understand-I still speak under reserve-concurrently with the proceeding under the criminal law. That is all the information I can give to my hon. friend at the moment. The Acting Minister of Justice may be able to give further information.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: STRIKE OF SHIP LABOUR IN LIVERPOOL CAUSES DELAY.
speechtext: I de- . sire to ask the Overseas Minister of Militia (Sir Edward Kemp) if the strikes in England have interfered, or are likely to interfere, with the repatriation of our Canadian soldiers, and if so, to what extent?

speakeroldname: Sir EDWARD KEMP (Minister of the Overseas Military Forces):
speakerposition: Minister of the Overseas Military Forces
maintopic: STRIKE OF SHIP LABOUR IN LIVERPOOL CAUSES DELAY.
speechtext: There have been strikes at the docks in Liverpool for the last ten days or more, and these have very seriously interfered with the embarkation of Canadian troops. No Canadian troops have been embarked from Liverpool since about the 14th inst. Our programme for the month of June contemplated the repatriation of some 55,000 Canadian troops. We brought back in the month of May about 55,000, and we had hoped that by the end of July, or even a little before that, we could get nearly all the Canadian troops back to Canada. I am inclined to the view, however, that the strikes will seriously interfere with that programme. It is feared, and it is possible, that the strike may extend to Southampton, where the very large ships sail from. However, I have information this morning which gives reason to hope that the strike may be settled to-day.

speakerposition: topic
Minister of the Overseas Military Forces
speechtext: There are a certain number of Canadian officers and men who have been in the vicinity of Archangel in Northern Russia. Twenty-two officers and 455 other ranks were due to arrive in England yesterday. There will be a few still to be repatriated, but we hope to bring them back at a very early date.

I notice from despatches which appeared in the press that negroes rioting in England cannot be deported on account of their British citizenship, but will be invited to leave that country by the offer of their passage money. I would like to know from the Government if any steps have been taken to ascertain whether any of these men are Canadians whom it is intended to return to Canada and if so, what action the Government intend to take as to their reception in this country when they arrive?

speakerposition: Minister of the Overseas Military Forces
speechtext: Do I understand my hon. friend to inquire whether or not these negroes are Canadian citizens?

I am asking if any steps have been taken by the Government to ascertain whether any of them are Canadian citizens, and if so what action the Government intended to take with respect to their return to their own country, and what disposition would be made of them as being undesirables?

speakerposition: Minister of the Overseas Military Forces
speechtext:
I did not gather
from the information which I read in the press that the negroes at Liverpool to whom my hon. friend refers were Canadian citizens. If there are any negroes in the Canadian army that are Canadian citizens they would be scattered throughout the forces- one or two here, and two or three elsewhere -and they would be treated exactly the same as other Canadian citizens.

My question is, have any steps been taken to ascertain if there are any Canadians among them? If so, how many are there and how is the Government going to dispose of them in view of their being undesirable?

speakerposition: Minister of the Overseas Military Forces
speechtext:
No such steps
have been taken with respect to the negroes referred to, because it was not supposed there were any Canadians amongst them.

On motion of Hon. C. C. Ballantyne {Minister of Marine) for the House to go into Committee of the Whole to consider the following proposed resolutions:
Resolved, That it is expedient to provide,-
1.	That the Governor in Council may, from time to time, advance and pay the Corporation of the Vancouver Harbour Commissioners, hereinafter called the "Corporation," such sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of five million dollars, as may be required to enable the Corporation to carry on the construction of works to provide such terminal facilities as are deemed necessary for the proper development and equipment of the harbour of V ancou ver.
2.	That during the period of construction of the works referred to in these resolutions, the interest payable on the debentures deposited with the Minister of Finance and Receiver General under the provisions of the Act to be based upon these resolutions, in respect of the construction of such works, shall be deemed to be money required to enable the Corporation to construct the said works, and to be a part of the cost of the construction thereof, and the said interest may be paid out of the said sum of five million dollars. The period of construction herein referred to shall begin on the day when the first advance is made on account of the said construction, and shall terminate on such date as the Governor in Oouncii shall fix and determine.
3.	That no construction of any works shall be begun, and no advances shall be made under the proposed legislation, until the necessary plans, specifications, and estimates in detail to govern the construction of such works have been submitted to and approved toy the Governor in 'Council.
4.	That applications for the said advances shall toe made monthly by the Corporation during the period of construction of said works, with statements detailing the total expenditure on any work in the month which the requested advance is to cover, and such other statements and information as the minister may require, and no payment shall be made on any application until the application has been approved by the Governor in Council.
5.	That the Corporation shall, upon any advances being made, deposit with the Minister of Finance and Receiver General, debentures of the Corporation equal in par value to the advance so made (which debentures the Corporation is authorized to issue by the proposed legislation), and each such debenture shall be for such amount as the Minister of Finance and

Receiver General shall prescribe. The debentures shall bear date of the day such advance is made, and shall be repayable within twenty-five years from the date of their issue. They shall bear interest at the rate of five per centum per annum, and such interest shall be made payable half yearly on the first day of July and the first day of January in each year.
6.	That the principal and interest of the sums advanced to the Corporation under the authority of the Act to be based on these resolutions, shall toe payable by the Corporation out of all its property and assets, and out of all its tolls, rates, dues, penalties and other sources of revenue and income, and shall rank as a charge thereon next after, and have precedence in regard to payment next after, the principal and interest of all debentures or bonds heretofore issued by the Corporation to the public and amounting to the sum of three hundred thousand dollars, said debentures or bonds having been issued under the provisions of chapter 54 of the Statutes of 1913.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will the minister please explain the resolutions.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This legislation is to empower the Government to loan to the Harbour Commissioners! for the port of Vancouver a sum of $5,000,000. I wish to explain that while there is a Board of Harbour Commissioners at Vancouver, no moneys have as yet been voted to them by Parliament. The terminal facilities at that port are very inadequate for shipping, more particularly in view of the fact that the Dominion Government now owns and operates what will soon be a very large mercantile marine. It will be necessary to build one or two deep-water berths there to accommodate not only the Government vessels but also the ships of other companies that ply to the port of Vancouver. It must not be understood that the $5,000,000 is to be expended immediately at this port. The Bill to be passed will merely be an enabling Act so that the money may be voted to the Harbour Commissioners and expended from time to time subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. Fees will be collected by the Harbour Commissioners of Vancouver, from wharfage dues and other sources, similarly as fees are now collected at the ports of Montreal and Quebec. The revenues so obtained will, it is considered, be sufficient to enable the Harbour Commissioners of Vancouver to pay five per cent on this loan.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would like the minister to give the House a statement, if he is in a position to do so, as to how we stand with respect to these different loans. , My experience is that they merely amount to giving money away; we never get that money back and we never get the interest.
The port of Montreal pays its interest.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The result is that these ports get more rapidly into debt. They come back for a further loan and the old debt and the new borrowings are incorporated in a new Act, and further sums advanced by the Government. Would the minister be kind enough to tell us how we stand with respect to these various loans made from time to time to ports such as Vancouver?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will be very glad, indeed, to give the hon. gentleman the information. As I have already stated, no advance whatever has been made to the port of Vancouver out of money voted by Parliament. A few years ago the Harbour Commissioners floated a loan of $300,000, but no extensive work has been undertaken there. I think we will all agree that the port of Vancouver is a very important one and that it is going to become more important, but we cannot accommodate the Government steamers, or the other vessels entering the port, unless piers are built. With regard to the port of Montreal, the Dominion Government has from time to time advanced sums totalling $26,485,000, the rate of interest on some of which loans has been three per cent and on others three and a half per cent. That port has always paid interest on these loans-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
-and will continue to do so. There is a Bill now on the Order Paper standing for second reading, under the provisions of which the rate of interest on loans to all harbours that are now under the direct control of the Minister of Marine will be advanced to five per cent, so that the port of Montreal in the case of any future loans will pay five per cent instead of three and three and a half per cent as in the past. I am quite satisfied, from an intimate knowledge of the affairs of the port of Montreal, that it will have no difficulty in meeting its interest even at the advanced rate. The port of Quebec, which is also administered by Harbour Commissioners, has been advanced the sum of $11,732,548, and the outstanding debentures amount to $1,150,000. I regret to say that the Harbour Commissioners of Quebec have never received sufficient revenue to enable them to pay any portion of the interest on the moneys that have been voted to them in the past. However, as Quebec is one of Canada's national ports, and its
maintenance is necessary in the interests of the whole country, the successive governments have deemed it advisable to incur the expenditure I have just mentioned. The only three ports that are under commission and to which loans have been, or will be, made, are Vancouver, Quebec, and Montreal.
Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR Mr. Speaker, could the minister tell us-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: This proceeding is most inegular. At the instance of the leader of the Opposition, it was understood that an explanation should be offered by the minister at this stage, but that any further questions should be put in committee. The motion is that I do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of the Whole to consider this resolution.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and the House went into committee on the resolution, Mr. Boivin in the chair.

This method of advancing money to the great ports of the country is much better than the method adopted in Halifax, where the Government themselves built the docks, and consequently all the incidental expenditure is a burden on the whole country. My idea is that the ports ought to pay the interest on these loans; the whole country should not be taxed for it. Of course, advances should be made with care, and I would like to be assured by the minister that the revenue of Vancouver Harbour is sufficient to warrant our embarking on this expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I went over this matter very carefully with the Vancouver Harbour Commissioners when they were here a few weeks ago. The revenue in the past has been very small, and would not meet the interest on the loan I am now proposing unless the dues were collected at that port as they are collected at Montreal and Quebec. I have instructed the Vancouver Harbour Commissioners to follow the same procedure as is followed at Montreal, and from the figures which they presented to me, they will have no difficulty in paying the 5 per cent interest on this loan.
It is my view that the various Harbour Commissioners ought to provide a sinking fund so that when these debentures fall due the Harbour Commissioners may themselves be able to take them up out of revenues collected. At present these debentures have to be taken up by the Federal Government when they fall due. T hope to make these advances real loans to the various Harbour Boards, so that they

shall not only pay the interest on them, but also meet the debentures when they fall due; and to that end I am taking steps to provide for a sinking fund at the various ports.

What was the
revenue of Vancouver harbour last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I had thought that this morning we would simply give notice that the resolution be considered in Committee of the Whole to-morrow; and therefore I have not before me, the statement which I have had prepared showing the present revenue and the estimated revenue for the ensuing year. I shall be glad to get the information for my hon. friend, but I point out that the revenue has been extremely small, because they had no interest to meet except the interest on the loan of $300,000.

When the Bill
based upon this- resolution is brought down, I would ask the minister to have the details' of the revenue of the port and of the tonnage which entered the harbour during last year.

I suggest that
the minister give us, at the same time, information respecting the arrivals and departures of ships from the port during that period.

How much is it proposed
to advance to the Harbour Commissioners during the present year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The programme has not really been decided upon. Representations have been made to me that these deep water piers should be erected at False Creek, on the Kitsilano Indian Reserve. Representations have also been made that that is not the most suitable place; that the piers ought to be built in Burrard Inlet-that is, in the harbour proper. I intend to go to Vancouver about the end of August to look over the ground, and after obtaining local and technical advice on the subject I shall recommend to the Government as to where these piers should be built. In any event, the expenditure during the next two years should not be more than $2,000,000. From what I learned from the Harbour Commissioners, I am under the impression that if they had two deepwater piers each of which would accommodate four ocean ships, that ought to be snough to carry them along for some years.

Will the loan of $300,000
already outstanding be paid off out ot this advance?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not before me the date of maturity of the loan of $300,000, but I understand that the bonds will not mature for some years, and I hope that by that time the Harbour Commissioners will be able to redeem them out of revenue. But if the revenues should Hot be sufficient to take these bonds up, they would have to be redeemed out of this loan.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am not opposed to the development of the harbour of Vancouver, or of any other national harbour, but I differ from my honourable friend (Mr. J. H. Sinclair); I believe that the harbours of all national ports, and all expenditure in connection with them, should be under the control of the Federal Government. I submit also that one or more engineers who are specialists, should be appointed to look after the necessary engineering in connection with the building of these docks. We cannot expect local commissioners to have the knowledge that is necessary to the proper carrying out of this work, because the harbour dues are not sufficient to enable them to engage such expert engineering services as are necessary , to the proper construction of these docks. In a sense, docks are world-wide property; they do not belong to us. in a way, any more than to any other part of the world, because ships from all parts of the world must use them. We must, therefore, have men in charge of the construction of these docks who have wide knowledge of matters of this kind, and it is impossible to expect that from a harbour commission.

While I do not
want to enter into any controversy with the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie), I still maintain my position that these great national ports can better be handled under local control than they can from Ottawa, and I think that is sound. We have the experience of the port of Montreal to fall back upon. It is the one bright spot in the management of the ports of Canada, and it has been managed in that way, that is, the Dominion Government have guaranteed the bonds where it is necessary to make large expenditures, and the port of Montreal has undertaken the full responsibility 'of paying the interest. It has continued to pay the interest for many years, and the whole arrangement has been very satisfactory. Who should know better how the port of Montreal should be run than the city and the people and merchants of Montreal? If you want to undertake to run the port of Montreal from the city- of Ottawa,

you will have the same kind of trouble we are experiencing in other directions. What is true of the port of Montreal is true of the ports of Quebec, St. John, and Halifax. If you are going to adopt a system of this kind, you will be following the example set in the port of Montreal. The same is true in all parts of the world. The great works on the Clyde are managed by the city of Glasgow. The Clyde has been dredged; great docks have been built; it is one of the cheapest and best ports of the world, and the whole matter is under local control. The city of Glasgow is proud of the work on the Clyde, and the whole matter is well managed. It could not be managed in the same way from London. The same thing is true of the ports of Liverpool, London, Hamburg and all the other great European ports, which are all under local control. I have no doubt, with our vast distances in Canada and the difficulty of managing the port of Vancouver from Ottawa, it would be a great mistake to introduce such a system as is suggested by iny' hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie).

I have no desire to delay this matter at this time, but I should be untrue to what I know to be economic truth if I did not, in a single sentence, dissociate myself from the somewhat antediluvian views of the leader of the Opposition and associate myself most heartily with the up-to-date and progressive views of the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair), founded as they are upon a long experience of shipping and some knowledge of what goes on at the ports of the world in this matter. The views of the leader of the Opposition on a matter like this are the growth of protectionist sentiment. The whole question of how far we are to have shipping depends upon the extent to which we believe in a protectionist tariff, and I can quite understand that it will 'be necessary for the national government to spend and keep on spending money upon our ports if we keep up our tariff, because after you have spent as much as you like, unless you have a fiscal policy to expand the commerce of the country, your expenditure on the ports will be largely in vain. I do not want to elaborate this much at this time; but there can be no doubt in the world, on the part of any one who knows anything about or Who has studied shipping and international trade that, on this matter, the views of my hon. friend from Guysborough are more progressive and more in accordance with the
trade facts of the world than those of the leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) has made a most effective reply to the leader of the Opposition, so that really I have not much to say. The hon. member for Guysborough has shown that he has a very thorough knowledge, not only of the ports of Canada, but of the ports of the world. I wish, however, to say in reply to the leader of the Opposition, that whether our ports are nationalized and operated by a local harbour commission, appointed by the Governor in Council, or whether the improvements in the various ports are carried out by the Department of Public Works, the Government in both cases is the owner. Everything within the boundaries of the *ports of Montreal, Quebec, and Vancouver which are under commissions at the present time, belongs to the Government, and the lands are Crown lands. I agree with the leader of the Opposition in so far as he goes in that direction, but where I would differ from him, in all friendliness, would be when he thinks that the improvements in those ports can be better carried out by the Department of Public Works than by a local commission appointed by the Governor in Council.
The personnel of these boards has been of a very high order. Our commissioners at the ports of Montreal and Quebec are among the leading citizens and most successful business men of those cities. It is also necessary at our big seaports for our commissioners to have a staff of the most highly skilled technical and engineering experts that can be obtained. With all due respect to the engineers of the Public Works Department, I say that there is not an engineer in that department to-day who

has as full a knowledge as is necessary of the development of ports to see that the improvements are of the character that the port demands, and that the work is properly carried out. When I had the honour of being one of the Montreal Harbour Commisioners during the big development years of that port we had to send to England and bring out an engineer from the port of Bristol to supervise the carrying out of the large plans. I am thoroughly convinced that when the harbour commissioners are appointed, if we get the proper men, and we have so far, the public interest will be better safeguarded and the work will be carried out more in keeping with the demands of the ports than if the work were done by the Department of Public Works. Some of the ports of Canada could tell a sorry story about the facilities that have been decided upon rather hurriedly without proper thought, but I will not go into that. I have, however, a very intimate knowledge of the mistakes that were made at the port of Montreal and other ports by the Department of Public Works, and to avoid such mistakes being made in the future I am a thorough believer in the Government appointing harbour commissioners to look after our ports. I am therefore in thorough accord with my hon. friend from Antigon-ish (Mr. Sinclair).

I should like to correct the impression which will probably go out to the country, coming as it does from the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), that the expenditure of money on our harbours is necessitated by the policy of protection. When a nation or the public assume a burden for the benefit of a private interest, that is protection. In England all the taxes in connection with the development of the ports of London, of Liverpool and of the Manchester ship canal, for instance, have been assumed by the public for the benefit of the shipping industry. It is a bonus or subsidy to encourage the shipping companies. Steamship companies are subsidized. Now that is pure unadulterated protection.

I am delighted to find that my hon. friend from Peterborough is in perfect harmony on this shipping question with the hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, but I have the gravest possible doubts whether the two gentlemen combined will be able to commend their views to this House and the country after a careful study of the methods by which

ports are managed and shipping is developed in Britain, and of the methods which I understand both of these hon. gentlemen to recommend.
The position is a very simple one. The leader of the Opposition knows, of course, that, to put it mildly, there is considerable shipping done in the port of Liverpool. 1 suppose it is, perhaps, the biggest shipping port in the world. Now, when one goes out of that beautiful harbour of Bedford Basin, as I have done more than once, on the beauties of which the leader of the Opposition is prepared to expatiate at any given moment, one cannot but be struck by the dearth of ships in Bedford Basin as compared with the plentifulness of ships in the port of Liverpool. The contrast is most striking to an observant traveller. The port of Liverpool has grown up as a free port, as I understand free ports. It has grown up under a system of free importation and free exportation-under a system of free trade. The want of trade in Bedford Basin, I think, can be traced to an opposite fiscal policy.
I understand that the leader of the Opposition's idea of a free port is a port to which all the nations of the world would be allowed to send their ships, provided they could get their goods over the tariff wall that is now preventing the admission of the goods. I want to tell my hon. friend that he may spend as much money from Ottawa as he likes to make Bedford Basin ten times more beautiful and effective as a harbour than it is to-day, but if he keeps his tariff wall high enough the shipping will not come, because commerce will not be profitable.
My idea of a free port is not a port in which ships do not pay dues. The ships that come to Liverpool harbour, of course, pay their dues to the Harbour and Dock Commissioners, and the Harbour and Dock Commissioners of Liverpool conduct the port where the greatest shipping in the world is done. My idea of a free port is a port where goods come in and go out freely, and on that free method of business will grow up a trade under which tne ships will oe only too glad, because of the profits they make by their ships, to pay any dues that come against tWin, and the central government will, of course, avoid responsibility for expenditure which is very much calculated to be altogether unproductive.
I am not opposed to spending money on the harbour at Vancouver. It is an equally beautiful port, and has every possibility of doing a world business. I, of all men, should be the last to be suspected of being opposed to the expenditure of money on
the port of Vancouver, but what I want is a fiscal policy which will make Vancouver another Liverpool, and I do not think that the hon. member for Vancouver will be opposed to that ambition for his citv, whether or not he quite agrees with me as to the method of doing it.
I want to reason with my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. I address him in the language of Scripture, if he will allow me to do so, " Come let us reason together " upon this question. Why the other Friday evening, before my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) had resigned the portfolio of Agriculture, and was getting through his estimates, there was some talk about cold storage facilities, and the leader of the Opposition made a speech to which I listened with interest and some degree of wonder, in which he showed that a million dollars could be most profitably spent by this Government in establishing a cold storage plant at the port of Halifax. Does my hon. friend think that there are no cold storage facilities at the port oi Liverpool ? Liverpool has abundant cold storage facilities, provided by the harbour and dock commissioners of Liverpool, and paid out of the shipping of the port. That is my idea of a free port. I put this to my hon. friend, who has a good head for business: If this Government is going to spend a million dollars upon a cold storage plant, is going to spend $5,000,000 upon harbour improvements elsewhere, and is going to go on handing out millions, how is he going to carry out the policy ol economy for which he voted the night before last, and where are we going to land if we launch into all these expenditures without making our fiscal arrangements so that we can do business to meet the expenditure in the only way it can be met. If my hon. friend was at all annoyed by the expression " antediluvian views," I withdraw it.
I applied it to his views, and I still hold that if those views are not quite antediluvian they are pretty ancient at this time of day, and when my hon. friend studies the question he will find that he lacks the current knowledge of men who have moved around the world and studied shipping. I tell him that in all friendliness because I want to get him on my side and he has been coming along splendidly. He says: I find this free trade protection question in everything I approach. Surely my hon. friend does not think that the fiscal policy of a country has not anything to do with its shipping. He would not take that position. What is the good of his bringing in a

reference to horse dealing? I think I could demonstrate to him that international horse dealing has had a very intimate connection with shipping up to now. No number of horses worth mentioning have yet been sent across the seas in aeroplanes, they have all gone in ships. Just another word to my hon. friend. He mentioned expenditures in recent years in this connection, to which I made no objection. I made very little objection to this Government's policy in time of war, and my hon. friend knows the reason. We did not send a man to France who was not vitally needed, and this Government did not make an effort during the war that was not called for to do Canada's full part in the struggle, and we are only in the position we are in internationally to-day, and the world is only freed from the menace that threatened it for several years, because this Government combined with all the Governments of the Allies to exert the last ounce of our ability in every possible direction.
That is why we are in the magnificent position to-day of being able to dictate terms to Germany. But I said the other day that one of the first duties of the Government now was to get away as far as possible from certain methods that were indispensable in war time, and that is my answer to my hon. friend who chides me for not having taken upon myself duties that w'ould have devolved upon him as leader of the Opposition if there was any real objection to he made to the expenditures in the last few years. I am not objecting to this expenditure now. I am only trying to throw out a few ideas by which we may be guided to see that we get profitable results from the expenditure.

It is well for us to
learn even from our enemies; the hon. member will agree with that. How did it come about that the year previous to the declaration of war the ports of Hamburg and Rotterdam exceeded the ports of London and Liverpool by 1,000,000 tons in shipping?

I have not alluded to that question and I would like to have documentary evidence of the truth of my hon. friend's statement,
iMr. BURNHAM: I can assure the hon. gentleman that it is true, and I should like him to consider the question.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I would point out to the hon. member for Red Deer a little incident that happened in this House during this session. I remember well that on the 25th of March a resolution was introduced into this House which, in my opinion after a long experience in this Parliament, was the most advanced resolution in the direction of free trade that was ever moved in the Parliament of Canada. I voted for the resolution and the hon. member voted against it. He will have to explain to his people, in the light of his advanced views, why when the question comes squarely before the House he refuses to support it. As regards the expenditure in Halifax, all I can say is, that this money which was expended there was voted long before the war which had nothing to do with it. The hon. member speaks of Bedford Basin. Bedford Basin is not really the harbour of Halifax. It is a magnificent inside basin, and while it is a part of the harbour it is not usually used commercially. If the hon. member had seen Bedford Basin during the last three years of the war I am sure he would have been very proud of it, not as a commercial harbour but by reason of the fact that no part of the Empire has served such an excellent purpose in connection with the war during its last three years. Bedford Basin has been simply crowded with vessels from all parts of the world coming there to receive proper orders on their voyages to various ports. I venture to say that no country in the world could by artificial means or by local expenditure produce such a magnificent body of water as Bedford Basin, and my hon. friend, with all the glories of the harbours of the Old Land, never saw anything in England, Scotland or Ireland in the shape of a harbour that could in any way compare with Bedford Basin. The harbour of Glasgow, of which we have heard so much, was made out of a field. Not so many years ago it was just a field and, all credit to the people of Glasgow, it was converted into a harbour. They had no harbour at all, but there was a large field

in the vicinity and they scooped it out and made a harbour of it, much to their glory. But we are not talking about that sort of thing but of the importance of improving the natural harbours we have, and it is no use my hon. friend comparing conditions in Liverpool and London, in a very small country where there are about 50,000,000 people and the oldest commercial establishments in the world, with a country of the vast area and distances of Canada with only eight millions of people. Great Britain is an old country- and Canada is new. Their resources and trade are developed; ours are not. We have to deal with primitive conditions and I think we are doing splendidly along international lines, and in that respect I intend to encourage the people of this country.
Mr. MICHAEL CLARK; May I reply to one specific point raised by the hon. member? I regret to occupy so much time of the Committee. In so far as the geography and the various characteristics of Nova Scotia are concerned, I confess my lack of knowledge and am prepared to sit at the feet of the hon. gentleman and be instructed by him. I should like some information as the internal management of our own harbours. Is it the intention that the grain elevators-at the port of Vancouver will be under the management of the harbour commissioners there?

The minister shakes his head. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must follow the good advice tendered by the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) a few minutes ago and ask the committee to return to the consideration of the resolution with respect to the Vancouver Harbour Commissioners.

I am glad the House has been afforded the. opportunity of discussing the facilities provided at the ports of our country. I am not opposed to expenditure for this purpose at Vancouver, or elsewhere, but I would draw attention to the fact that the port of Quebec, as stated by the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) is able to take care of the grain traffic of the West. Therefore? that port should also get its share of the money voted for improving these ports and be developed in such a manner as not only to handle the grain trade but to make a proper use of the Transcontinental Railway

and carry out the purpose for which it was built, thereby enabling traffic to avail itself of the shorter route and consequently permit of a reduction in freight rates, WTe had the pleasure of a visit to Quebec last fall from the Minister of Public Works who came to inspect the port and the works for the improvement of the Transcontinental terminal. The minister expressed the opinion that those works were a tragedy. The minister was perfectly correct in using that term bearing in mind the manner in which the works have been handled at Quebec of late years. The country has made large outlays in Quebec to develop the port, but after the present Government came into office everything was changed, despite the formal promise of the Prime Minister in 1913 that the works at Quebec for the proper equipment of the port and the Transcontinental terminal should be carried on not only in the interest of the port and province of Quebec but in the interest of the entire Dominion. In his opinion at that time Quebec occupied a unique position and should receive a share of the favours of the Federal Government.
The Prime Minister was accompanied by several of his ministers-Hon. L. P. Pelletier, Hon. Mr. Hazen, Hon. Mr. Cochrane, and others, all of whom endorsed the policy of the Prime Minister with regard to the development of the port and harbour of Quebec. The Prime Minister at that time laid the corner stone of the St. Malo workshops and inaugurated the works on the St. Charles river, upon which the Government has expended, as was stated by the Minister of Public Works a few days ago, $1,600,000. If my information is correct, the Government have acquired the plant and equipment from the contractors, Quinlan and Robertson, for the amount of $300,000, and although they are spending $15,000 to $20,000 a year to keep it in order, it is lying there doing nothing. At a cost of over $2,000,000, the Government have acquired a property which has a frontage of over three miles along the St. Lawrence river and that property is lying there idle. To a stranger coming down the river to Quebec this property gives every evidence of being in the last stage,of decay. The Prime Minister said that the port should be developed; that grain elevators should be constructed to take care of the grain from the West, and that proper terminals should be built. It was the intention of the Government to spend millions of dollars in the development of the port; the works inaugurated in 1913 were only the beginning of an extensive

programme of development. But not a single cent is being voted in the Estimates this year for any improvement at Quebec, although the St. Malo workshops are idle and freight cars and rolling stock which are in need of repair are taken from the Eastern division to Winnipeg or Transcona, a distance of 1,350 miles. That is the way Quebec has been treated by this Government. I take this opportunity of airing some of the grievances of the citizens of Quebec in this regard; I am not opposed to any expenditure which the minister proposes for the development of any of our ports.
The 'CHAIRMAN: Before the minister replies to the statement of the member for Quebec county (Mr. Lavigueur) I must direct the attention of the Committee very seriously to the fact that the recent discussion has been entirely out of order. To be strictly within the rule, the discussion should have related only to the port of Vancouver; but it has wandered far afield, and while I think it is only just and right that the minister should be granted the privilege, by unanimous consent, of replying to the charges which the hon. member has made, I would ask hon. members thereafter to keep more strictly to the rule. Mr. Chairman, we have the finest port in the world-

that is more in favour of developing harbours and harbour navigation and foreign^, shipping than I am; but there is one harbour on the St. Lawrence which I think is the best in Canada with the exception of Vancouver which I do not know anything about, and the harbour I refer to seems to have been forgotten. I would ask the minister if this policy, which is to be extended to Vancouver, is to cover one of the best harbours in Canada, at least the best of all on the St. Lawrence, and if improvements are to be made to the harbour of Three Rivers. I will not discuss the merits of the harbour of Three Rivers, because I know the Minister of Marine has developed the harbour of Montreal and has made it one of the best harbours, if not the best harbour in the world, but at the harbour at Montreal there are difficulties which are not to be found at the harbour of Three Rivers, and the same difficulties are to be found at Quebec. There are no tides at Three Rivers, and it is not necessary to keep men at the hawsers when the tide flows out or in to lengthen or shorten them, and there is no necessity for tugs. As this is practically laying down a policy on the part of the Government, if the harbour commissioners are to be on the same footing as at Montreal, and if the Government is going to render assistance by lending money for improvements on various harbours, I submit the best harbour on the St. Lawrence is Three Rivers, and I desire to ask the minister if this policy, which seems to be that of the Government, is to be extended to that particular harbour, and, if so, within what time we may expect to see the result of this new policy.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. Mr. Ballantyne (Minister of Marine), the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution-Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend, the Canada Shipping- Act, and to provide:-
1.	That a transfer or a mortgage or a transfer of a mortgage of a British ship registered in Canada to a person not Qualified to own a British ship, or to a foreign controlled company, shall not have any effect unless the same is approved by lie Minister of Marine and Fisheries on behalf of His Majesty.
2.	That any person who makes or purports to make such a transfer, mortgage or transfer of mortgage without this approval shall, in

respect of each offence, incur a penalty of a fine not exceeding five thousand dollars or imprisonment for any term not exceeding five years, or both fine and imprisonment, and such penalty may be imposed either upon summary conviction or upon indictment.
3.	That the expression "foreign controlled company" shall mean any corporation,-
(a)	where the majority of the directors, or persons occupying the position of directors by whatever name called, are not British subjects; or
(b)	where the majority of the voting power is in the hands of persons who are not British subjects, or who exercise their voting powers directly or indirectly on behalf of persons who are not British subjects; or
(c)	where the control is by any other means whatever in the hands of persons who are not British subjects; or
(d)	where the executive is a foreign controlled company, or where the majority of the executive are appointed by a foreign controlled company.
A corporation shall not be deemed to be a British subject for the purposes of this resolution unless it is established in and subject to the laws of some part of His Majesty's dominions or of some British Protectorate, and has its principal place of business therein.
4.	That the minister may require any person who is the owner or mortgagee of a British ship registered in Canada, or who applies to be registered as the owner or mortgagee of a British ship registered in Canada, to furnish to him such particulars as appear necessary to him for the purpose of ascertaining whether or not that person is, or is a trustee for, or otherwise represents, a foreign controlled company, andi, in the case of a corporation, may -also require the secretary, or any other officer of the corporation performing the duties of secretary, to furnish those particulars.
5.	That if any person fails to supply such particulars as it is in his power to give when required, or furnishes particulars which are false in any material particular, he shall be guilty of an offence and shall incur a penalty of a fine not exceeding five thousand dollars or imprisonment for any term not exceeding five years, or both fine and imprisonment, and such penalty may be imposed either upon summary conviction or upon indictment.
6.	That where, after the passing of the Act based upon these resolutions, any person who is the owner or mortgagee of a British ship registered in Canada ceases to be a British subject or becomes a foreign controlled company, that ship, or, in the case of a mortgagee of a ship, the interest of the mortgagee shall be subject to forfeiture under Part I of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1894.
7.	That in these resolutions, unless the context otherwise requires, any reference to a ship shall include a reference to a share in a ship.
S. That the Act embracing this proposed legislation shall continue in operation during the present war and for three years after the conclusion of peace.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have read this resolution somewhat carefully, and it suggests to me that there may be special cases with which the minister intends to deal. I should like the minister to explain to the committee if there are any cases in which ships have found their way into the hands 238J
of wrong parties. It is, of course, the common law of this country that foreigners can own almost every kind of property except a ship. [DOT] If it is found that ships have got into the hands of foreigners, as this would appear to indicate, it might be well to explain. It would be better, perhaps, in cases of that kind to deal specifically with any one specific case that may have gone wrong than to create a general policy. I do not think the old common law should in any way be departed from. It should be made abundantly clear that foreigners are not qualified to own any interest in a British ship.
Mr. BAIiLANTYNE.: The object of this resolution is to enable the Government to control, for a period of three years after the declaration of peace, the transfer of a British ship registered in 'Canada to a person not qualified to own a British ship or to a foreign controlled company. Such restriction naturally involves the mortgaging of a ship and the transfer of such mortgage. I might also explain that the Imperial Government passed the necessary legislation for this purpose in 1915, the Act being entitled " The British Ships (Transfer Restriction) Act, 1915." The Act is valid for three years after the declaration of peace, but it does not apply to ships registered in Canada. Shortly after war broke out, by order in Council, it was made necessary for those who wanted to have transfer of registry or transfer of mortgage to apply to the Minister of Marine to get such authority. Orders in Council were passed, one	on the 9th	March, 1915, and
another on the 9th October, 1917.
After the signing of peace I have very good authority for doubting whether these Orders in Council will remain valid, and this Bill has been introduced with the ob-jecf of ensuring the authority we had under the Orders in Council to control the transfer of registry and of mortgage. We have a good deal of ship construction going on at the present time, and I think hon. members will agree that it is in the best interests of the country that we should keep a watchful eye on this tonnage, not only now, but during the reconstruction period of three years, let us say. Great Britain is doing that, and I think we should also. In answer to the question of the leader of the Opposition as to how many transfers or registry or mortgage have taken place, in the year 1917 the number of vessels transferred to foreigners or neutrals allowed to be owned to foreign-controlled companies was 73, and the mortgages allowed to

such interests during the same period amounted to 12; in 1618, 138 vessels and 9 mortgages. The British -Act which I have just referred to, and which is known as the Transfer Restriction Act of 1915, will also remain in force for three years after the declaration of peace. There is no intention to embarrass or interfere in any way with shipping, but we think it wise to exercise this control for three years after the war. We must look after our Canadian tonnage, and this is one of the safest ways of doing it.

I assume that the minister intends to introduce a Bill founded on this resolution.
Mr. BALLAiNTYNE: I have it here.

The minister is
proposing to change the law on a very important question. Prior to the war a British subject owning a ship in Canada was at liberty to sell it without asking anybody's leave. If he could sell it to advantage to a foreigner he did so, and there is no good reason in time of peace why that should not be the case, but when the war broke out we needed all our tonnage for our own use, and a change was very properly made. I question the wisdom of making the present provisions permanent. I do not know what the minister's idea is, but I would think we ought to go back to peace conditions, when it was open for a man to buy or sell a ship without the minister's approval. Is there any good reason why we should embody these provisions in a statute? If this is intended only as a temporary measure, it is all right. Are we to be in the position permanently that the sale of a ship is to be made only with the consent of the authorities at Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think it wise that foreigners should control any of our shipping, either at this time or for three years after the war. This Bill, if passed, will remain in effect only for that period. Prior to the war it was unnecessary either in Great Britain or here for any one to have the Government's approval for the transfer of registry or mortgage. They merely went to the registrar of the port and got the transfer made, afid they can get the transfer now without any undue delay from the Minister of Marine, if he thinks it is in the national interest. We have not in mind the British subject so much as the foreigner. It would certainly be unwise to let any of our shipping pass into foreign hands during the reconstruction period.

That is why the provisions are made applicable for three years after the war. When that time is up I presume England will go back to the position she was in before the war, and Canada will do the same. We are simply guarding against foreigners getting possession of Canadian tonnage.

"Foreigners" is rather a broad term. The United States is our nearest neighbour, and a good many of the ships that are being built in the Maritime Provinces to-day are being built for sale to the United States. That is a profitable business to our people. I presume the minister does not intend to interfere with the building of ships in Canada, even if they are not to be placed on Canadian registry. The minister tells us that the leave of the department is freely given; if so, that is satisfactory, but I would be opposed to restricting the sale of a ship unless it is absolutely necessary. If a Canadian citizen owning a ship can sell it to a foreigner and replace it by a better one, why should he not be allowed to do so?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I understood my hon. friend from Antigonish to say that a man could build and sell a ship in Canada before it is put on the Canadian register. That is not my understanding.
Mr. BALLAiNTYNE: No. Before the war, if a man wanted a Canadian ship put on the United States register, he would apply to the registrar of one of our principal ports and the transfer would be made without any difficulty. Now the approval of the Minister of Marine has to be obtained. We are only too glad to consent to the transfer. I have approved of at least a dozen transfers to the United States and other countries. We want to encourage the development of shipping in every way, but we must see tha* during the reconstruction period none of our shipping passes out of our hands against the national interest.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The hon. member for Antigonish did not get my point. I understood him to say that Americans are giving orders for the building of ships in Nova Scotia, for instance, and when those ships are finished they take them off to the United States as they might take anything else that was built. I understand the law to be that when you build a ship in Canada she must be measured and registered and classed in this country. She has to comply with the law before she can be taken to any other country and sold.

That is also my understanding. The law is strictly enforced that a ship must be registered before she is sent to the United States, but it is only a formal matter to get the registry transferred from one country to another in peace times. My point was that there should be no interference by the department that would have the effect of discouraging the construction of ships. As the minister says, we want to encourage shipbuilding. It is only a matter of detail placing a ship on Canadian registry and then transferring her to American registry the next day.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Quite right.
Resolution reported, read the first and second time and concurred in.
Mr. Ballantyne thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 148, to amend the Canada Shipping Act founded on the resolution.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. Alinister of Alarine (Hon. C. C. Ballantyne) has handed me a printed copy of Bill No. 149, to provide for a loan not exceeding $5,000,000 to the Vancouver Harbour Commissioners, founded on the previous resolution, and moves that it be now introduced. Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.
At one o'clock the House took recess.
The House resumed at three o'clock.
ArONTREAL AND QUEBEC HARBOURS-RATE OF INTEREST ON LOANS.
On the motion of Hon. Mt. Ballantyne, Bill No. 135, respecting the rate of interest to be paid on loans.by His Majesty to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal and Quebec, read the second time and the House went into Committee on the Bill.-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-five per cent interest to be paid on advances made after 1st April, 1919:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I notice that the two
harbours referred to are those of Montreal and Quebec; is that sufficient for any other place?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The only harbours that have had any moneys voted to them have been those of Montreal and Quebec and the advances were made to these harbours at the low rate of 3 and 31 per cent. But now that money is higher it was thought better to raise the rate of interest to 5 per cent. The resolution that passed the committee this morning relating to the Vancouver harbour provides that the rate of interest shall be 5 per cent. These are the only three ports which are under commission at the present time. If any other port comes under a commission the rate of interest to be charged will be 5 per cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does this Bill give the minister authority to lend money to other ports are 5 per cent without coming back to Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: All I have to say about the rate of interest is that the Government should not be losing money on it. If the money can be obtained at 5 per cent it is fairly good business to lend it at that rate. We are not looking to make any money but I rather suspect that it costs the Government more than 5 per cent to get money to lend. If it costs us more than 5 per cent to get the money it is poor business to be lending it at less than it costs us.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think a fair average would be 5 per cent. The Government have paid as high as 51 per cent for a certain amount but it seems to me that if we charge the harbour commissioners 5 per cent it should be a fair and reasonable average.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Ballantyne the House went into Committee on Bill No. 39, to amend the Fisheries Act, 1914, as amended by the special committee. Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-license fee for British Columbia increased from $50:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The first amendment is, that in line 1 of paragraph 2, the word "such'' shall be replaced by the words "a salmon cannery." Then a sub-clause has been added as follows:
The annual1 price for a salmon curing license shall be $50.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I might explain that when this Bill was introduced it was referred to the Special Committee on Marine and Fisheries and they have considered it and referred it back with the amendment which has just been read. The object of the Bill is to raise the annual canning license fee in British Columbia from $50 to $500 and also the additional charge according to their fish catch. This Bill as it is now meets with the approval of all the British Columbia members. I discussed it myself with those interested in the cannery business some months ago. My reason for recommending it is twofold; first of all, I consider that the fee of $50 per year is altogether too low in view of the volume of the business that each one of the canneries does. The Royal Commission which was appointed in 1017, and which was composed of Mr. Sanford Evans, Mr. Thompson and Mr. Black, recommended in their report that the cannery fee be raised to $1,000 per year. My departnfent thought it advisable to make the fee $500 and impose the additional fee according to the catch *which, we think, will make nearly $1,000 tfor the 92 canneries in British Columbia. It will also enable my department to increase its revenue which is very sorely needed. In the administration of the service on the Pacific coast, there is a deficit of $135,000 and it is believed that the changes which we are making with regard to the revenue will wipe that deficit out. On the merits of the case I think we are justified in raising the fee.

The facts before the committee disclosed that the salmon fishery of British Columbia is a monopoly, that the department has restricted the issue of licenses to something like 94 or 95 and that when a license is granted to anybody it is bought up by the monopoly. It is worth a good deal of money. That is not a healthy condition of affairs. I may say to the minister that the same attempt was made in the Maritime Provinces in regard to the canning of lobsters. The packers were endeavouring to control the number of licenses knowing that if they could control the number of licenses they could build up a monopoly. But the Department of Marine and Fisheries at that time refused the request of the packers and threw the business of canning open to any man who could qualify. The buildings and plants are inspected and care is taken to see that the goods are well packed.
Every man who can put up the money to build a cannery and carry on packing
[The Chairman.]
is allowed to do so. If this were the procedure in the province of British Columbia we would not have the condition which exists there to-day where a business which should engage the activities of a great many manufacturers is in the hands of a few people who keep up the prices of canned salmon and control the fishermen. The fishermen oift there are said to be, to all intents and purposes, the bond slaves of the packers; they do not own their own boats, or anything else, they simply do what the packers tell them to do, they have no initiative of their own and no ambition -at least that is true in the case of most of them-to make any progress. IHas the minister considered the question from this aspect, because he must have all the facts before him. It is not a new question, it has been before the House for a great many years, but despite that fact nothing has been done. I would suppose that at the present time when the price of food is so important it would be a wise policy to throw the whole industry open and allow any one who can qualify for packing salmon to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: When I came into office what is known as attached and unattached licenses were issued and each one of the canneries was allowed so many. It was represented to me that this was not a fair and equitable plan and that fishing licenses should be open. Accordingly I gave notice to the canneries that commencing with the first of January, 1919, the licenses would he open to everybody. Therefore it is not true that the canners control the fishermen to the same extent as when they were able to hold a certain number of licenses. When attached licenses were issued, the canners made their arrangements with the fishermen and supplied them with boats and equipment, but with open licenses the conditions are different. I should explain, however, that the object of restricting the number of canneries is not to create a monopoly, but to conserve the salmon. If a monopoly exists now it certainly existed in past years, and to allow the license 'fee to remain at $50, if the canneries do enjoy a monopoly- which I am not prepared to admit is the case, but for argument's sake we will admit it-is to allow them a further advantage. But the reason for restricting the number of canneries was in the interest of the conservation of the salmon.

Would not the
preservation of the salmon be better con-

trolled by shortening the fishing season, than by refusing to grant licenses to pack?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It costs a great deal of money to erect one of these canneries and I think we must pay due regard to the expenditure incurred by the people engaged in the industry. I do not for a moment say that the present policy will be continued permanently, but after going into the matter very carefully with the fishery officials on the coast, as well as the officials here, I do not see that any monopoly exists. I think we have enough canneries for the time being, but nevertheless we are granting other licenses from time to time, and during the last few days I have agreed to two additional. I wish to assure the members of the committee that no monopoly will be allowed to exist on the Pacific coast while I am minister, and I certainly do not consider that such a thing exists at the present time. My object is to make these canneries pay a reasonable license for the privileges that they enjoy. We ought not to grant a license for the paltry sum of $50, which is practically giving it away, when we should receive something like $500 or $1,000 a year.
I notice there is a charge of four cents for each case of forty-eight one-pound cans of salmon. Is the minister, or his inspectors, convinced that these cans contain one pound of meat?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That question has been very much debated in the House, not so much with respect to salmon as to lobsters. It is rather a technical point. Where the can contains liquid or pickle as-well as meat I would say yes. Where the contents consists of dry meat only, I would answer in the negative.
Are there inspectors to examine the pack and ascertain what the amount of meat in each can is?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There are inspectors and the matter is governed by regulation as well. The contents of the can are supposed to weigh sixteen ounces to the pound, but that includes liquid as well as dry meat.
Is there any regulation governing the dry meat content of the can?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is, but I do not have it under my hand at the moment. If necessary I will obtain a copy for the hon. gentleman.

If the minister doubts the existence of a monopoly on the Pacific coast, I must refer him to the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. McIntosh) who made a speech to the Fisheries Committee and produced evidence which satisfied myself and everybody present on that occasion that there is one.
Mr. iMcKENZIE: I deem it my duty to bring to the notice of the minister some protests which I have received from four or five of the large packers in British Columbia against an increase in the license fee. The minister did not say so, but it might be inferred that the canners were behind the increase and that it was done for the purpose of creating a monopoly. Whether or not there is a monopoly, I cannot say, but at any rate I have received these protests against the increase in the fee so that the parties concerned in them are evidently not favourable to the advance. I am not quite clear that it was ever the intention of Parliament to tax any industry for its own promotion. I think that is protection and I must gain the good will of my friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) by opposing it. I want the fisheries-as well as anything else in regard to which we can take action-made free, and I do not think it is good policy to tax any industry for its own individual support, although I would favour the appointment of any necessary official for the proper supervision of the packing done in these factories and tax the industry for the purpose of meeting the expense. Of course, we are now imposing taxation for war purposes in many directions and we have to do a great many things contrary to our ordinary policy by reason of it, but the taxation in this case is not attributable to the war; it appears to be a policy for the purpose of getting revenue, and I do not think there is any justification for such a proposition. As regards the lobster canneries in the Maritime Provinces, the object in imposing the license fee is not to secure revenue. The purpose was to give the Government some control over those establishments, in order to see that they were properly equipped and maintained and that it would not be open to any one to start packing lobsters in a haphazard way that might result in giving a bad name to the industry.
The idea was not to raise revenue, but to exercise proper control over the industry. I do not think there should be one rule in connection with lobster packing and another in connection with salmon packing; there should be no exactions except such

as I have mentioned. It is a mistake for the minister to try and get a revenue in this way.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This request certainly did not come from the canners. When I read the recommendation of the Royal Commission that the fee be increased to $1,000 a year, and when I looked into the matter myself-saw their balance sheets and found out what was the volume of the business and what the profits were-I thought at once that the fee was far too low. When the canners were here some months ago I told them that I proposed to increase the license fee, and that I did not want to do it without first consulting them. They were not particularly pleased, but they unanimously agreed to it. I understand that since then some of these canners have wired their objections to the leader of the Opposition. I do not blame them as business men for trying to get a license at the lowest possible rate; but it is my responsibility as minister to see that, having regard to the volume of their business and the privileges which they enjoy under their licenses, they pay a reasonable fee, From my knowledge of business charges, I do not consider that $500 a year, with the additional tax on the fish catch, is at all out of the way. Our fisheries inspectors in British Columbia inspect the canneries and the processes of packing, and see a proper weight is put into the cans; the inspection is of a most thorough and efficient nature. I should be derelict in my duty if I allowed the gentlemen who own canneries to have licenses at $50 a year, and I strongly recommend the approval of the fee of $500.
What license fees do the canners of lobsters pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A Bill respecting the lobster industry will be before the House for second reading in a few days, when it is reported from the Select Standing Committee on Marine and Fisheries, and I shall be glad to discuss that matter then. If we are to get through with the business which we have to do and prorogue in the near future, I think we had better stick to what is now before the Committee.

I think that the question is perfectly in order. I want to make a comparison between the fees paid by lobster packers and those which are paid by the salmon packers. It is not fair that the minister should answer me in that manner.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) is perfectly in order. The hon. member wants to know how the fees 
which we are fixing in respect of the salmon fishing industry compare with those applicable to another industry very closely allied to salmon packing.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not desire to withhold any information from the hon. member; I simply wished to save time, and if the Chairman rules that the question is in order, I shall cheerfully give the hon. member the information that he wants. For lobster packing the charge for license is $5 for the first hundred cases and $2 for each hundred cases thereafter. The provision reads:
The annual fee for any such license shall he at the rate of $5 for the first 4,800 pounds of canned or cured lobsters or fraction thereof canned or cured under such license and $2 for each additional 4,800 pounds or fraction thereof canned or cured under such license.
Of course, lobster packing is quite different from salmon packing; the volume of business is much greater in one case than it is in The other.

Subsection 2 of this clause provides that in addition to the $500 license fee, the packers shall be required to pay a fee of three cents for each case of 48 cans; consequently the license fee in the case of salmon packing would appear to be very much greater than that which is paid by the canners of lobsters. It seems to me that this license fee of $500 will prevent the man of small means from going into the canning business; it certainly is putting the business of canning salmon in British Columbia into the hands of the big interests. In the interests of common people the license fee should be much smaller so that any one may can salmon who is able to raise enough money to start a factory.

We were told
in the committee that about ninety four licenses had been issued to canners in British Columbia, and that no new ones were being granted. By what authority is the department refusing to grant additional licenses to persons who wish to can salmon in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The department is
not refusing to grant licenses; as I said a moment ago, I granted two additional cannery licenses within the last few days. Discretionary powers are vested in the' minister as to the number of canneries there shall be in British Columbia; but no minister would act without consulting his officers in that province and taking into consideration the situation as a whole.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister says that after looking over the business of these companies, examining their balance sheets and observing the profits that they make, hejias come to the conclusion that he should get more money from them for the general purposes of the country. The price of salmon is soaring, as is the price of practically all other foods, and here was an opportunity for the department to say:	You are charging extraordinary
prices; you have practically a monopoly of .this business; you are not charged high license fees, and you should not sell this excellent food product at such a high price. If, therefore, he had asked the can-ners to reduce their prices, that course would have been more acceptable to the people than the taking of surplus profits by way of fees.
-Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR:	Is there any
restriction against the importation of canned salmon into Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not know of
any, outside the customs tariff.

I have seen the
statement in the press that the canners have large quantities of canned salmon in stock and that they have requested that steps be taken to prevent tbe importation into Canada of salmon until they have disposed of the stock which they have on hand. I am anxious to know if any steps have been taken in that direction.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No steps have been taken in that direction, nor will any be taken. It is well known that the canners have a large stock, but certainly neither the Government nor the Department of Marine are going to take any such steps as those suggested by the hon. member. As regards the price, inasmuch as the United States produce 82 per cent of the canned salmon and Canada a very small fraction as compared with our neighbour to the south, the canners have to arrange their prices in competition with the United States. Salmon, of course, advanced in price during the war as there was a big demand and a large amount was shipped overseas for our soldiers, but now the war is over, the canners find themselves with very large stocks, and as a natural consequence the price will have to drop.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Is this amendment I
find added to the Bill a new section? It reads:
The annual fee for a salmon curing license shall be $50.
1 do not quite understand the difference between the two kinds of licenses. One is for $500 and the other for $50.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The $500 license is for a salmon cannery, and the $50 is for what is called a salmon curing establishment of which there are only two in British Columbia. They catch the spring salmon and cure them; they do not can salmon. One is curing; the other is canning.

speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
