speakerposition: topic
subtopic
subtopic: SECOND BEADING OF DIVORCE BILE MOVED BY MR. NICKL.E.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. WILLIAM FOLGER NICKLE (Kingston), moved the second reading of Bill No. 77, respecting divorce.
He said: On the 20th February, of this year, I gave notice of the following motion:
That, in the opinion of this House, the procedure under which divorces are granted by Parliament and the consequent unreasonable expense thereof are so unsatisfactory besides being prohibitive to the great majority of the people of Canada that a committee of members should be appointed to enquire into the existing procedure and to report, as promptly as possible, what more satisfactory procedure should be provided.
At the time I gave notice of that motion, it was my intention to introduce the subject to the House in an academic way and not by way of a Bill. As, however, time progressed and the notice of motion was not called, I received from various parts of the country such assurances that public opinion was ripe for the discussion and probable passing in this House of a Bill respecting divorce, that I decided to proceed by way of a Bill rather than by way of a motion. I might say that among the recommendations to which my attention was directed, was this recommendation from the Women's Advisory Committee of the Committee on Repatriation:
That the present system of granting divorce in Canada ibe abolished and that a National Mobile Divorce Court be established, which, at the request of, and by arrangement with the individual provinces, would sit in the provinces and adjudicate Claims for divorce. Thn Women's Advisory Committee consider that legislation on Divorce should be national in scope and character, but that the privilege and right of availing themselves of such legislation and such a national court should be reserved to the discretion of the individual provinces and should not be imposed on any of them.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The Women's Advisory Committee fear that social conditions resulting from the war may give rise to many claims for divorce and to presentation of insufficient grounds for same, and they apprehend that if the question of divorce be left for settlement to the provinces, it may lead-not only to varied legislation but also to lack of a uniform standard in the application and interpretation of the divorce laws. If this were the case, the present high standards of family life in Canada would be jeopardized.
A Mobile Court, national in character, interpreting a National Divorce Act and administering the laws connected therewith, would be not only a national safeguard of the bulwark of the nation-its homes-'but, by reason of its mobile character, would also save expense to individuals and to the provinces, being accessible to applicants on request of the province at periods of the year to be fixed by mutual arrangement by the National and Provincial Governments.
The Women's Advisory Committee again emphasize the need of making arrangements in legitimate cases of dftmrce whereby the man or woman of average means be not prohibited from obtaining same because of the excessive cost of legal and court fees.
I also received numerous resolutions passed by representative Army and Navy Great War Veterans and Grand Army of Canada organizations* with reference to the domestic condition in which many of their members found themselves-, requesting that some steps be taken to establish a national divorce court or a national divorce law. It would unduly take up the time of the House if I were to read many of the letters I received in regard to individual cases, but there is one -so pathetic in form and so generic in spirit I received from a returned soldier, that I think I would not be unduly taking up the time if I read it to the House. The letter is addressed to myself, and reads as follows:
Dear Sir,-In reading several papers I see where you are trying to revise our present divorce laws. I am one of the unfortunate chaps who would benefit by your good work.
I am a returned soldier and was three years away from Canada and spent considerable time in the trenches. I am writing this letter to ask you to do all in your power for to help the returned lads. A large majority of them have been unfairly treated by unfaithful wives while overseas. In fact there is a score of cases here alone, and other cities are just as bad1.
Just imagine the feelings of a chap who, on coming back to Canada, finding his home gone, everything he ever possessed gone. I was comfortable when I went overseas. It was humble, but was home to me. I came home in December last and everything was gone, my child deserted. I had no place in the large country and the money I made over to my wife was keeping a worthless drunk instead of clothing my child.
Now my allowances were $13 a month (thirteen dollars a month) while in the army and I had to buy a little to eat while overseas as the army food was far from enough to ease our hunger. 'So where can I, out of that sum, pay $1,500 to be separated from one who has

wronged me. We fought for liberty and justice and I fail to see where we unfortunate chaps are getting it.
I tried to get my wife to come and help me to get a home together again, and as soon as I got her settled and gave her some money she tried to kidnap the child which the authorities took from her owing to her immorality and went to live with this chap again and I believe, married him. She has no reasons for doing this as she told the judge I was a good man to her and had nothing against me. So you can plainly see it was done wilfully. I have a little girl six years old that was neglected shamefully in my absence.
Sir, I appeal to you to help us. I think it is right in the sight of God for you to take this step as his punishment for adultery is death.
Hoping this letter will help you in your good cause and hope you have success.
This is typical of many communications that I received, and moved somewhat by the communications and resolutions that reached me I decided I would attempt to secure the passage by this House of a divorce law.
I quite appreciate that in some of the provinces of the Dominion divorce has not at the present time any legal status, and to that particular aspect of the case I propose in a few moments to direct the attention of the House. To understand the position of divorce in Canada it is necessary that one should trace, possibly briefly, divorce practice and legislation insofar as it pertains to iGreat Britain and to Canada. The argument must necessarily be legal, and at certain times what I have to say and may say may touch men in their religious and conscientious beliefs, but I shall try as far as in me lies to avoid saying anything that would be insulting to the conscience or belief of any man who may differ from me on this essential question, and I would urge on those who have conscientious beliefs in reference to divorce, who believe that marriage is a sacrament and that it should not be dissolved, that they endeavour to see conditions as they are in Canada to-day, and to treat us who differ from them with the same consideration that I shall endeavour to show them this afternoon.
As I said, divorce may be divided into two classes. First, there is a partial divorce, which is technically known to lawyers as a divorce a mensa et thoro, that is, a divorce from bed and board, a separation, but not a dissolution of the marriage. Such a divorce when obtained does not give either of the parties the right to marry again, nor does it bastardize the children subsequently born. It may be granted at the suit of either husband or wife on misconduct being shown by either, provided

either is of the opinion that the misconduct of the other has made it impossible for them to live together as man and wife.
Then there is the complete divorce technically known to us lawyers as a divorce a vinculo matrimonii, that is, a severance of the marriage tie. This divorce differs from the divorce a mensa et thoro, or the judicial separation, in that the parties to such a divorce, if obtained, have the right to re-marry, and any children born to the woman thereafter will he illegitimate children provided she has not married again. Divorce a vinculo matrimonii, or complete divorce, divides itself in the law into two classes:	First, there is annulment, which
strictly speaking is probably not a divorce at all, because it is a judicial declaration by the court that there never has been a legal marriage and if there never has been a legal marriage there could not be a severance of the marriage tie. Leaving aside for a moment that technical distinction, the court does regard annulment of the marriage, and it has been regarded, as a divorce, and the effect of such a decree is that children born of that marriage are regarded after the judicial decree has been obtained as having been illegitimately born. Divorce, as we ordinarily understand the term, is really a rescission of the marriage contract. It is a dissolving of the tie that binds the man to the woman or the woman to the man, and is granted in consequence of some supervenient conjugal transgression which, having risen subsequent to the marriage, makes it impossible for either party to live with the other. It is here that I find it necessary to touch for a moment on the religious aspect of the case. Prior to the Reformation the causes for the annulment of marriage, as recognized by the Roman Catholic church, were greater in number by far than were recognized by the law of England since the time of Henry VIII. Mr. W. B. Northrup, once a member of this House, and now the Clerk of the House, in 1914 gave a very exhaustive and all-embracing address in this House in reference to the legal status of divorce in the British dominions, and I quote from his speech when I direct the attention of the House to the evidence of Monsignor Moyes given before a commission of 1852 of the English House appointed to look into this question. In his evidence he said:
The impedients which are held by the Catholic Church to be diriment or nullifying are the following:
1.	Error, as to person.
2.	Condition (if A marries B, a slave, believing B to be free).
3.	Solemn vow of chastity on entering religious order, made before consummation of marriage.
4.	Consanguinity to third degree.
'5. Crime (if A during a former marriage with B has committed adultery with C, with promise of marriage after death of B, and if A or C has attempted the life of B, the marriage of A and C is null).
6.	Disparity of worship, viz., marriage of a Christian with a non-Christian.
7.	Duress or violence affecting liberty of consort.
8.	Holy order to which is attached obligation of chastity.
9.	The bond of preceding marriage (if either party have a husband or wife still alive).
10.	Public decorum (if one of the parties is solemnly or publicity bethrothed to another person) .
11.	Madmess or amentia (viz., imbecility precluding reasonable consent).
12.	Affinity.
13.	Clandestinlty.
14.	Impotency.
15.	Rape.
For any one of those causes the Roman Catholic Ecclesiastical courts prior to the Reformation would have granted an annulment of marriage. They would have preserved their position, as a church, that marriage was indissoluble, but they would have said that such causes as those to which I have directed the attention of the House would have been a reason, not for the dissolution of the marriage, but for the declaration that the marriage never had existed. They would have declared an annulment and the parties would have been free to marry again. However, the Reformation came in England, and Henry the VIII by 38 Henry VIII, Chap. 38, restricted the grounds on which marriage might be dissolved by annulment, and since the passing of that statute the only reasons that will permit, according to English law, a marriage to be annulled are: relationship within the forbidden degrees, a previous marriage, corporal imbecility, or mental incapacity.
Now what was the effect of that? It was this: Prior to the Reformation those who desired a divorce !could obtain it, often easily, by annulment, or much more easily than they could after the passing of the statute to which I have just referred, and the Roman Catholic Ecclesiastical courts would recognize it. But after the Reformation, when the grounds of annulment had been tremendously curtailed, those who found themselves joined together in an unfortunate matrimonial alliance, found themselves unable to free themselves, so to. speak, from the entanglement, and men did as they

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
have always done when oppressed by a harsh law, they endeavoured to find some way by which they could get around the law, and I want to trace very briefly for the information of the House just what took place in England.
As I said in my opening remarks, by the tenets of the Roman Catholic Church marriage is a sacrament, and as such is indissoluble. As I have pointed out, the Reformation brought a change in the pritish point of view, and after the Reformation marriage was no longer regarded by the English Church as a sacrament, a divine institution alone, but as a civil contract, and there was therefore rio reason why the contract, provided there had been a breach of the terms in reference to which the parties had entered into it, should not be terminated or dissolved. How was this to be done? The first great outstanding case is the one commonly known as the Parr case, the case of the Marquis of Northampton, in 1548. That case is referred to at some length in Macqueen's Practice, of the House of Lords, pp. 468 and 469, where Bishop Burnet is quoted as follows:
*'11 January, 1548	(1 Edward VI.) The
Marquis of Northampton, brother to the Queen Dowager, had married Anne Bouchier, daughter to the Earl of Essex, the last of that name; but she being convicted of adultery, he was divorced from her; which, according to the law of the Ecclesiastical Courts, was only a separation from bed and board.
That was divorce a mensa et thoro to which I directed the attention of the House on rising to my feet.
Upon which divorce it was proposed, in King Henry's time, to consider what might be done in favour of the innocent person when the other was convicted of adultery. So, in the beginning of King Edward's reign on the 7th of May, a commission was granted to the Archbishop of Canterbury,the Bishops of Duresme and Rochester, Dr. Ridley and six more, ten in all, to try whether the Lady Anne was not by the word of Good so lawfully divorced that she was no more his wife, and whether thereupon he might not marry another wife. This being a new oase of great importance, Cranmer resolved to examine it with his ordinary diligence; and searched into the opinions of the Fathers and Doctors so copiously that his collection about it grew into a large book (the original whereof I have perused), the greatest part of it being either written or marked and interlined with his own hand. This required a longer time than the Marquis of Northampton would stay; and, therefore, presuming on his great power, without waiting for judgment he solemnly married Elizabeth, daughter to Brooke, Lord Cob-ham. On the 28th January information was brought to the Council of this. So, he being put to answer for himself said he thought that by the word of God he was discharged of his tie to his former wife; and the making marriage indissoluble was but a part of the Popish
[Mr. Niokle.J
law, by which it was reckoned a sacrament; and yet the Popes, knowing that the world would not easily come under such a yoke had, by the help of the Canonists, invented such distinctions that it was no uneasy thing to make a marriage void among them ; and that the condition of this (the Reformed) church was very hard if, upon adulteries, the innocent must either live with the guilty or be exposed to temptations to the like sins, if a separation only was allowed, but the bond of the marriage continued undissolved. But since he had proceeded so far before the delegates had given sentence, it was ordered that he and his new wife should be parted; and that she should be put into his sister the Queen Dowager's keeping till the matter was tried, whether it were according to the will of God or not, and that then further orders should be given in it. Upon this the delegates made haste; and the whole question was, divided into eight queries, which were put to some learned men (who these were does not appear), and they returned their answer in favour of the second marriage, and, by consequence, confirming the Marquis of Northampton's marriage to his second wife; who, upon that, was suffered to cohabit with him."
That is the first recognition in an important case of the position of the Reformed Church. Four years later (6 Edward VI) the Marquis secured an Act confirming his second marriage. This was not a divorce bill. It only declared that the adultery of his wife, followed by the ecclesiastical sentence, entitled the Marquis to take a second wife. And let me direct the attention of the House to that point. It was necessary that the ecclesiastical sentence in divorce a mensa et thoro should be obtained before Parliament took action. The ecclesiastical sentence having been obtained, it was held that the Marquis was entitled to take a second wife and the Act was so passed. The principle on which the Act passed assumed the jurisdiction ol the Church Courts to dissolve the marriage. The Act did not divorce the parties, but merely declared them to be already, by the ecclesiastical sentence, sufficiently divorced to admit of the Marquis marrying again.
In the following year Mary, as the House knows, a Roman Catholic sovereign, came to the Throne and the Act confirming the marriage of Parr was repealed.
Cranmer's commission, appointed pursuant to statutes of Henry VIII, to order and compile such laws ecclesiastical as should be thought convenient, proceeded with its inquiry. It was composed of 16 ecclesiastics, and advised that in cases of adultery (sec. 1); malicious desertion (sec. 8); long absence (sec. 9); deadly hostility (see. 10); prolonged ill-treatment (sec. 11); the marriage should be dissolved, with liberty to the injured party to marry again. If both parties were guilty of adultery, no divorce (sec. 17). Husband not entitled to

divorce if he incited his wife to adultery (sec. 16).
It was also recommended that the remedy of divorce a mensa et thoro should be entirely abrogated and done away with. This report was completed in the reign of Edward VI. Owing to his premature death the whole scheme fell to the ground, and was never crytallized into legislation. The result was that in England under the Reformed Church from 1550 to 1601 marriage was held to be capable of being dissolved.
In 1597, the ecclesiastical authorities (105th Canon) pronounced the following doctrine:
Forasmuch as matrimonial causes have been always reputed among the weightiest, and therefore require the greatest caution when they come to be handled and debated! in judgment, especially in oases wherein matrimony is required to be dissolved or annulled; we strictly charge and enjoin that in all proceedings in divorce and nullities of marriage, good circumspection and advice be used, and that truth may as far as possible be sifted out by the depositions of witnesses and other lawful proof, and that credit be not given to the sole confessions of the parties themselves, howsoever taken upon oath, either within or without the court.
In all sentences pronounced only for divorce and separation a thoro et mensa, there shall be a caution and restraint necessary in the said sentence that the parties so separated shall live chastely, and neither shall they, during each other's life, contract matrimony with any other person.
The reason I direct attention to that canon is this: That canon apparently laid down the doctrine, as I have read it, that the Church would require that a divorce having been obtained from an ecclesiastical court, during the life of each neither party should marry. That cannon proceeded:
And for the better observance of this last clause the said sentence of divorce shall not be pronounced until the party or parties requiring the same shall have given good and sufficient caution and security unto the court that they will not in any way break or transgress the said restraint or prohibition.
Clearly, therefore, by implication, the bond being required that no remarriage would take place, it necessarily follows that the ecclesiastical courts regarded the ecclesiastical divorce as of such a character that the parties could legally remarry, but the pecuniary penalty was imposed to prevent [DOT]marriage in so far as the penalty would prevent it. If any gentleman in the House cares to follow this matter more fully than I have time this afternoon to deal with it, I would suggest that he read Bishop Cozer's argument, which is reported in State Trials, page 1331.
Up to this time-summarizing my remarks -the ecclesiastical courts of the Reformed Church recognized the marriage tie as being capable of dissolution. The Roman Catholic Church regarded marriage as a sacrament and therefore refused to recognize divorce. From 1500 to 1601 the Reformed Church held that marriage could be dissolved, but in that year a new doctrine was introduced into the church courts. Foljambe's case, 44 Elizabeth, 1601, came for decision before John Whit-gift, Archbishop of Canterbury who, on the advice of the most eminent divines and civilians of the period declared that a second marriage, the first wife living and divorced for adultery, was invalid, and re-asserted the doctrine of matrimonial indissolubility. And the law in England until 1857 (and in Canada excepting in those provinces in which there are divorce courts) was, therefore, that marriage was indissoluble.
In 1604, the Statute of Bigamy was passed by Parliament, making that offence a felony. In this way, jurisdiction lor the offence was taken from the ecclesiastical to the civil courts. There was an express provision in the Act that it should not extend to any person divorced by a sentence of the ecclesiastical court.
[Now the very fact that that exception was incorporated into the statute affecting bigamy makes .it reasonably clear that the civil law of England regarded parties divorced by ecclesiastical courts as having had the matrimonial tie dissolved and that they were in a position to marry again.
If that had not been so the exception in the statute of bigamy would not have been passed.]
The historical review makes it clear' that husbands were trying to find a tribunal that would, in consequence of adultery, free them and permit a second marriage, the first wife living. One of the chief grounds of the desire for a remedy was to prevent the fathering of illegitimate children on the husband as followed from a divorce a mensa et thoro. The next effort to get relief from the ecclesiastical courts was the Lukenor case. In this case an Act was obtained to bastardize the issue born while the wife, against whom sentence of divorce had been obtained, continued to live in open adultery, but it did not dissolve the marriage bond or allow the innocent party to marry again. The Act simply laid down the principle that the ecclesiastical courts having pronounced a decree of divorce a mensa et thoro, and the wife continuing to live in adultery, and there being a possibilty of subsequent issue, Parliament was of the

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
opinion that the husband should have removed from him the responsibility of having to father the children born under such circumstances.
The next case is the Lord Roos case in 1666, in the reign of Charles the Second. It established the principle that Parliament recognized that the marriage tie could be dissolved. Lord Roos had obtained an ecclesiastical divorce for adultery. The previous Act of 1666 which he had obtained had declared any subsequent children to be illegitimate. He stated that there was no possibility of posterity on his part to support the family in the male line unless he was entitled to be put in such a position that he could again be married and that the children of the subsequent marriage would be legitimate.
In 1669 there was a declaration by the English Parliament to the effect that Lord Roos might marry during the lifetime of his former ecclesiastically divorced wife and that subsequently born children would be legitimate. This was practically a statement that according to the parliamentary belief of that day the marriage tie could be dissolved. Th6 argument of that time and the position taken by Parliament is very amply stated in MaoQueen's Parliamentary Practice, and it bears so cogently on conditions of to-day that I think I would not be unduly taking up the time of the House if I should read what is there said, because I realize that the question that is before us this afternoon for consideration is one that vitally touches the social life of the people, and is one upon which many people feel very strongly, not only for social, but also for conscientious reasons. I am endeavouring to show the House that the procedure in England exactly parallels what has been the procedure in Canada, and, by the analogy of what took place in England, that the establishment of national divorce courts is the solution for the difficulties as we find them in Canada to-day.
In MacQueen's Practice, pp. 472 and 473, it is stated:
"The successful argument of Bishop Cozens in that important case (Lord Roos' Case) gives us a very clear conception of the principles on which the Legislature originally interposed to grant relief in this form. The Bill was vehemently opposed by the Roman Catholic members of both Houses. It was also opposed by persons who, though professing the reformed religion, were yet of opinion, that the allowance of divorce a vinculo-
That is a Bill of absolute divorce.
-would be productive of injurious consequences to the public morals. The advocates of the

measure, on the other hand, while they abjured an unlimited freedom of divorce, at the caprice or volition of the parties, contended that divorce a vinculo might safely be conceded for the Scriptural causes of adultery and malicious desertion; which, according to God's ordinances, dissolved the marriage contract. By the Mosaical institutions, the terms of divorce were "Be thou expelled from me, and free for anybody else." Under the dispensation of the New Testament, a husband whose wife was dismissed for fornication might take another wife. The words of our Saviour on this head, as recorded in the fifth and nineteenth chapters of the Gospel according to St. Matthew, had rendered it a matter of necessary and irresistible implication, that a second marriage, under such circumstances, was valid and unobjectionable. As to the supposed inconveniences that might arise from awarding divorce, the supporters of the Bill maintained, that greater inconveniences would arise from refusing it. They urged, that to declare marriage positively indissoluble, under all circumstances, and in spite of all descriptions and degrees of conjugal transgression, would be not only unscriptural, but highly impolitic; that marriage, a holy estate, intended for the comfort and enjoyment of both the sexes, ought not to be converted into an instrument of punishment; that to withhold divorce from an injured husband was but to tempt him to commit sin, and to give his wife an opportunity of palming a spurious offspring upon her husband. And, finally, they maintained, that if a second marriage were not allowed in cases of adultery, the consequences would be dangerous to society; for the spouses condemned to a hateful and inextricable union, would be apt to resort to practices against each other, worse in their consequences and example to society than any evils that could possibly arise from a moderate and Christian exercise of the remedy, of divorce. These arguments prevailed	"
The first example of the actual dissolution of the nuptial tie by Parliament was in the case of the Countess of Macclesfield, 1687-8. Skilful opposition had prevented an ecclesiastical divorce a mensa et thoro being obtained. The circumstances of the domestic life were scandalous and most flagrant as any one may prove who cares, to read the case. A judgment had not been obtained for damages against the respondent who had seduced the wife. The facts in reference to the whole case may be obtained by looking at the report of the Matrimonial Commission of 1852, page 261. The proceedings in the House of Lords were so new, and the issue was so unusual that a protest was made by the Duchess, in which she said:
" My Lords, I had rather stand charged for High Treason before your Lordships than with this Ignominious crime. In the charge for High Treason, the manner of trial and the ways of proceeding are known, and so is the punishment. But your Lordships are now creating new ways of proceedings, and a new law to punish me, and this for a crime supposed and alleged to be committed seven years past, in another reign, and after public indemnities in many sessions of Parliament."

That was the first case in which Parliament declared a dissolution of the matrimonial tie. The next case was the Duke of Norfolk's case 1699-1700. The ecclesiastical courts had again refused a divorce, but damages had been recovered against the adulterer. I again read from the report of the British Commissioners, page 260, what Bishop Burnet said:
"The matter was one of great importance, and it occasioned great and long debates in this and the former session of Parliament. It related to the Duke of Norfolk, who had found his wife guilty of adultery, and did move for an Act of Parliament dissolving his marriage, and allowing him to marry again. In the latter ages of Popery, when marriage was reckoned among the sacraments, an opinion grew to be received that adultery did not break the bond, and that it could only entitle to a separation, but not such a dissolution of the marriage as gave the party that was injured the right to marry again. This became the rule of the Spiritual Courts, though there was no definition made about it before the Council of Trent (1565). At the time of the Reformation, a suit of this nature was prosecuted by the (Marquis of Northampton. The marriage was dissolved and he married a second time; but he found it necessary to move for an Act to confirm the subsequent marriage. In the reformation of the ecclesiastical laws that was proposed by Cran-mer and others in King Edward's time, a rule was laid down allowing of a second marriage upon divorce for adultery. This matter had lain asleep above a hundred years, till the present Duke of Rutland , then Lord Roos, moved for the like liberty. At that time a sceptical and libertine spirit prevailed; so that some began to treat marriage as a civil contract, on which the Parliament was at full liberty to make what laws they pleased; and most of King Charles's courtiers approved of this, hoping, by this doctrine, that the King might toe divorced from the Queen. The greater part of the bishops apprehending the consequences that Lord Roos's Act might have, opposed every step that was made in it; though many of them were persuaded that, in the case of adultery, when it was fully proved, a second marriage might toe allowed. In the Duke of Norfolk's case, the Bishops were desired to give their opinions with their reasons; all those who had been made during the present reign were of opinion that a second marriage in that case was lawful, and conformable both to the words of the Gospel and the doctrine of the primitive church, and that the contrary opinion was started in the late and dark ages. But all the bishops that had been made by the two former kings were of another opinion, though some of them could not well tell the reason why they were so."
Now what is the summary. In Luke-nor's case, a parliamentary declaration of illegitimacy was desired and obtained.
In Lord Roos's case the object was to continue the succession and probably the peerage in the male line.
In the Macclesfield and Norfolk cases redress was asked which the ecclesiastical courts had refused.
In 1701 though, a change took place and it is as a result of that application to Parliament that our parliamentary practice has the existence that it has to-day. In 1701 a man by the name of Ralph Box made application for a divorce from his wife Elizabeth Eyre and to enable him to marry again. No appeal had been made to the ecclesiastical courts. The Bill was passed, adultery of course being proved, and the precedent was established, and from that time on until 1857 the British Parliament constituted itself a court for granting divorce a vinculo matrimonii, that is a complete divorce. The right of Parliament to grant the divorce was recognized, but in the rudest and most inconvenient manner as the procedure was a judicial one by legislative process, which is the procedure we have in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and in those cases that are brought to us from the other provinces, in the Parliament of Canada to-day.
From 1700 to 1775 only five divorces were granted by the English Parliament. From 1715 to 1775, sixty divorces were granted, from 1775 to 1800, 74 were granted, and from 1800 to 1852, 110 were granted. The better the right came to be recognized, the greater the number of applications that were. made and granted. The British Parliament laid down the principle that-" they would grant a divorce to a man when he established adultery on the part of his wife, but they took a somewhat different position in reference to an application made by a woman. The first application that was made by a woman to the British Parliament for divorce was made in 1801. To 1857-and the reason I use that date is because it was the date at which divorce courts were established in England -as a result of the report of a commission which was appointed, to which I shall shortly direct attention-only four wives obtained divorce a vinculo. These were only granted where there was aggravation. The wife had to show adultery and also other aggravating circumstances. The unfaithfulness of the husband and the wife are alike criminal from a religious point of view, although there is a great difference socially, as members of the House will readily see, in reference to the amount of injury that might be sustained, when the wife commits adultery as compared with a case in which the man commits adultery. When a woman commits adultery there is the possibility of spurious issue being created, and there is certainly a confusion of progeny, and of the parentage of the children likely to result. When

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
a man commits adultery that is not so likely. The result was that the British Parliament laid down the doctrine that in reference to an application for divorce on the part of a woman the divorce would only be granted when there were aggravating circumstances. When divorce was asked by the man the divorce would be granted providing the woman had committed adultery. In 1909 a British commission looked into this matter and the result of its consideration is to be found in the Bill which I have introduced into this House in which I put the man and the woman on a parity in reference to the right to obtain divorce. I give them the same right in the courts as this Parliament and the country recognizes -that if adultery is proved and the court is satisfied upon the point, the divorce is to be granted to the woman just as readily ae to the man. The British Commission found and said:
" No satisfactory solution of the problem, which is raised as to the personal relations between husband and wife, can be found, except by placing them on an equal footing, and by declaring that, whatever grounds are permitted to a husband for obtaining a divorce from his wife, the same grounds shall be available for a wife in a suit against her husband. It may be safely left to a woman to consider whether she will exercise her rights, and it may reasonably be expected that, as has been proved by actual experience in Scotland, physical, social, pecuniary, and other considerations will have their natural effect, and lead to such nights not being exercised, at any rate in the great majority of cases, without such good and sufficient reason as will meet with the approval of relations and friends of the wife."
If any member of the House cares to follow this matter further, I would direct him to the proceedings of the Divorce Cbmmis-sion of 1912, at page 24, and if they wish to read further in relation to the matter, they might refer to Lord Lyndhurst's appeal to the House of Lords in 1857.
Lord Brougham also, and I shall not take up the time of the House in reading his remarks, dealt with the matter very fully. His observations may be found on pages 446 to 448 of his speeches.
This testimony was given before the commission appointed by the British Government in reference to the law of Scotland by Lord Salveseb (senior judge in the Outer House of the Court of Session, Scotland), in giving his evidence:	[DOT]
" That he regarded the Scottish law, by which, since the Reformation, no difference has . existed between the sexes, as better than the English, that there is no demand for a change and that he was expressing the views of the Scottish Bench on the subject. He considered that the Scottish law very much

conduced to the morality of husbands and the peace of families."
So far, I have endeavoured to show the House how the parliamentary procedure had grown in England, and I have only to impress upon the members present that the argument seems to lead irresistibly to the conclusion that husband and wife should be treated in the same way in relation to a divorce being granted, providing adultery is proven. I have also endeavoured to show to the House by what manner divorce applications reached the House of Lords in the British Parliament.
Until 1798 there was no well-defined procedure .in the British Parliament, but in that year Lord Loughborough established a definite method of procedure. The British Parliament determined that before a divorce would be granted an application first had to be made for divorce a mensa et thoro and all proceedings brought into the House of Lords on oath. They also said that a judgment must be obtained for damages against the adulterer, or evidence must be brought to show that proceedings had actually been prosecuted, or that there was some good reason to the contrary where these proceedings had not been taken. What was the result of this? The result was that tremendous expense was incurred, and it was found that the parliamentary divorce courts were practically closed to those who had not very substantial means. An English divorce at that time would cost about £1,000, and if it was a contested case and many witnesses the expense ran to three or four times that amount. A climax in British national life was reached in 1845. A prosecution was laid by the Crown against a man by the name of Hall, who was charged with bigamy. I referred a few moments ago to the address that the present Clerk of the House delivered in 1914, and I am taking advantage of his work when I quote from sometning he said as reported at page 822 of the Hansard of that year.
Speaking of the case of Regina vs. Hall, Mr. Northrup read the following sentence pronounced by Mr. Justice Maule:
Prisoner: You have been convicted upon clear evidence; you have intermarried with another woman, your lawful wife being still alive. You have committed the crime of bigamy. You tell me, and indeed the evidence has shown that your first wife left her home and her young children to live in adultery with another man. You say this prosecution is an instrument ot extortion on the part of the adulterer. Be it so. I am bound to tell you that these are circumstances which the law does not in your case take notice of. You had no right to take the law into your own hands. Every Englishman is bound to know that when a wrong is done,

the law, or perhaps I should rather say the constitution affords a remedy. Now, listen to me, and I will tell you what you ought to have done. Immediately you heard of your wife's adultery you should have gone to an attorney and directed him to bring an action against the seducer of your wife. You should have prepared your evidence, instructed counsel, and proved th^ case in court; and recollect that it was imperative that you should recover, I do not mean actually obtain, substantial damages. Having proceeded thus far, you should have employed a proctor and instituted a suit in the ecclesiastical courts for a divorce a mensa et thoro. Your case is a very clear one, and I doubt not you would have obtained your divorce. After this step your course was quite plain ; you had only to obtain a private Act of Parliament to dissolve your marriage. This you would get as a matter of course upon payment of the proper fees and proof of the facts; you might then have lawfully married again. I perceive, prisoner, that you appear scarcely to understand what I am saying to you, but let me assure you these steps are constantly taken by persons who are desirous to dissolve an unhappy marriage ; it is true, for the wise man has said it, that "A hated woman, when she is married, is a thing that the earth cannot bear," and that ''A bad wife is to her husband as rottenness to his bones." You, however, must bear this great evil, or must adopt the remedy prescribed by the constitution of your country. I see that you would tell me that these proceedings would cost you £1,000, and that all your small stock in trade is not worth £100. Perhaps it may be so. The law has nothing to say to that; if you had taken these proceedings you would have been free from your present wife, and the woman whom you have secondly married would have been a respectable matron. As you have not done so, you stand there a convicted culprit, and it is my duty to pass sentence upon you. You will be imprisoned for one day.
The report in the London Times gives this additional sentence:
And as you have now been in jail since the commencement of the assizes, your term is more than expired; you are free.
That case so shocked the common sense of the British people that they began to look about to see if something could not rectify the condition, with the result 'that in 1850 a Royal 'Commission was appointed " to inquire into the present state of the law of divorce and more particularly into the mode of obtaining a divorce a vinculo matrimonii That commission reported in 1853, the inquiry having been mainly directed to the substitution of a proper legal tribunal for the procedure by private Act. The result was the Act of 1857, under which, by section 27, divorce is permitted on the following grounds:
A. On the petition of the husband, adultery.
B. On the petition of the wife-
1.	Incestuous adultery;
2.	Bigamy with adultery ;
3.	Rape;
4.	Sodomy;
5.	Bestiality;
6.	Adultery coupled with such cruelty as without adultery would have entitled her to a divorce a mensa et thoro (the equivalent in the Ecclesiastical Courts of judicial separation) ;
7.	Adultery coupled with desertion, without reasonable excuse, for two years or upwards.
By section 30, the absolute defences are:
1.	Denial of facts alleged in the petition.
2.	Connivance (such conduct by one party to the marriage as to show that he or she corruptly intended that the other party to the marriage should commit adultery).
3.	Condonation (forgiveness of a conjugal offence with full knowledge of all circumstances followed by cohabitation).
4.	Collusion (presenting or prosecuting the petition by agreement between the parties to the marriage or their agents).
By section 31 the discretionary defences are:
1.	Adultery of the petitioner.
2.	Unreasonable delay in presenting or prosecuting the petition.
3.	Cruelty to the other party to the marriage.
4.	Wilful desertion or separation without reasonable excuse from the other party before the adultery complained of.
5.	Wilful neglect or misconduct such as to have conduced to the adultery complained of.
Various subsequent amendments have been made from time to time, but it is not necessary that I should direct the attention of the House to them, because the Divorce Act of 1857 is the Act which is in effect in certain provinces to which I shall shortly refer, having been introduced by the introduction into these provinces of the British law as it stood in 1870.
What was the result of all this? The result of this enactment was that the moral right-not the legal right-to legislative favour as recognized by the granting of the parliamentary divorce was crystallized into a legal right enforceable at law; and that is what I am arguing for in introducing the Bill which this afternoon I ask the House to approve.
It is well known to every member of this House that any person who has the means and cares to present a petition to Parliament, if he is in a position to demonstrate that adultery has been committed, has a moral right to divorce, but in Ontario and Quebec, because we have no divorce courts, there is no legal right to a divorce. In various other provinces, as I shall shortly show, there are divorce courts with varying jurisdiction and a varying practice. I believe that the time has come when in this Canada of ours we should, in connection with this all-important social question, have one Canada-wide, all-embracing law, so that the same practice, and the same right shall be enjoyed by all domiciled Canadians, no matter in what province they happen to live.

Let us see what the Canadian law is- because if members of this House realize the patch-work condition of the Canadian law they will realize that I am not trying to obtain, by the enactment of this divorce law, the adoption of any new principle, so to speak, but that I am trying to turn what I may call patch-work legislation and patch-work rights into some co-ordinate scheme of equality of right for the people.
By section 91, subsection 26 of the British North America Act the jurisdiction in reference to legislation touching marriage and divorce is retained for the Dominion Parliament. The British North America Act, by section 129, also determined that existing laws should remain in force in the province in respect of those subjects that fell under Dominion jurisdiction until they were changed by some legislative authority which - was competent to do so.
Now, what is the position in regard to divorce in the various provinces? Prince Edward Island, by a statute of 1836, 5 William IV, chapter 10, has a divorce jurisdiction; the Lieutenant Governor and five members of the Executive Council may grant a divorce. There has been no change since Confederation. Only one divorce, in 1835, was granted by the Lieutenant Governor in Council, other divorces in respect of that province having been obtained from the Dominion Parliament. No case has arisen under the Act since the Island entered the Federal Union. It is apprehended that if a case does arise there may be some difficulty in deciding whether the powers given by the Act are exerciseable by the Governor General and Council under section 12 of the British North America Act, 1867, or by the Lieutenant Governor and Council under section 129 of the same Act. Hon. gentlemen who wish to follow this subject further may do so by reading Gemmill on Divorce, page 37. The grounds for divorce in Prince Edward Island are adultery, im-potency, consanguinity.
In Nova Scotia a divorce court exists, under 29 Victoria, 1866, chapter 13. The grounds are adultery, impotence, cruelty, consanguinity.
In Quebec, a divorce court does not exist; Parliamentary procedure is necessary. The same is to be said of Ontario.
Now I come to Manitoba, and it is very interesting to watch the development here, because the Dominion Parliament, probably without knowing it, created divorce courts in Manitoba, Alberta, and Saskatchewan and the North West Territories; and if lion, gentlemen are interested and care to follow
[Mr. Niolde.l	^
me, I shall endeavour to show how that was done.
In Manitoba it has been decided by the case of Walker versus Walker, 1917, 28 Supreme Court Reports, that the Manitoba courts have jurisdiction in divorce, because the Dominion Statute of 1888, chapter £3, section 1, introduced the English law as of the 15th of July, 1870. As the House will remember, a few moments ago I showed that in 1857 a divorce court was established in England, and the iSupreme Court of Manitoba held that the divorce law of England, as it existed in 1870 by virtue of the Act of 1857 in Great Britain, introduced into Manitoba the law of England in reference to divorce without introducing the procedure, and the Manitoba court adopted the English law with its restrictions in reference to the rights of women, although the English procedure was not introduced, and the Manitoba courts have developed a procedure, so I understand, of their own.
In Alberta and Saskatchewan the Dominion Statute of 1887 introduced the law of England as it stood on the 15th July, 1870, just the same as the law was introduced into Manitoba, and exactly the same argument applies. There has been a case before the courts recently, the case of Board versus Board, which is reported in the Supreme Court cases of Alberta and is now in appeal before the Privy Council, to determine whether or not the introduction of the law in England as it stood in 1870, that is the Matrimonial Act of 1857 of Great Britain, is the law of Alberta, and it seems to me it is inevitable that the conclusion must be reached that that law was introduced. The Supreme Court of Alberta has held that the law is effective and that Alberta has a jurisdiction of its own. The Manitoba courts held the same thing, and, therefore, in the light of a British Columbia case to which I shall shortly direct the attention of the House, it would appear to a lawyer to be impossible that the same principle shall not be held applicable to Alberta as the Privy Council held to be applicable to British Columbia. What will be the effect? British Columbia will have divorce jurisdiction; Manitoba will have jurisdiction; Saskatchewan will have jurisdiction; Alberta will have jurisdiction; Nova Scotia will have jurisdiction; New Brunswick will have jurisdiction, and Prince Edward Island will have jurisdiction. Ontario and Quebec, the two greatest provinces, will be the only provinces that will not have a judicial jurisdiction and will be the only pro-

vinces from which the residents must come to the parliamentary forum in case a divorce is desired. The British Columbia case is that of Watts versus Watts, which is reported in the English law reports, 1908, Appeal Cases at page 573, in which the House of Lords, the court of final jurisdiction, held that the English law, that is the law of 1857 with the amendments as they stood at the introduction of the law into British Columbia, was introduced into British Columbia, and, therefore, the British Columbia courts have jurisdiction in regard to divorce. New Brunswick has a court for divorce and matrimonial causes similar to that in England. The grounds are, adultery, impotence, consanguinity. It is specially provided, however, that no decree on the ground of adultery shall affect legitimacy of any child subsequently born, that is prior to the divorce court.
What is the history of the Canadian parliamentary divorces? The first case was in 1839. This was an application by J. Stewart to the Parliament of Old Canada, and it is interesting to note that the Governors General of Canada from 1867 to 1878 were expressly instructed by the British Government that they were not to consent in Her Majesty's name to any parliamentary divorces. Confirmation of that statement may be haid in Bourinot's prefatory note to Gemmill on divorce.
Let me summarize to the House just for a moment or two what the divorce law and the divorce practice is in this country. In the first place in those provinces in which a divorce court existed prior to Confederation, that is in the Maritime Provinces, jurisdiction is vested in the provincial courts and apparently, generally speaking, husband and wife are on a parity. In Ontario and Quebec there is a moral right to a divorce providing adultery is shown on application to the Parliament of Canada, but there is no legal tribunal to which an applicant domiciled in those provinces can apply. But when you go to Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia, you have the British law by which husband and wife are not on a parity. The husband can obtain a divorce from his wife by simply proving adultery, but if the wife wants a divorce in the legal tribunals in those four provinces, she has to prove not only adultery but aggravating circumstances. If she cannot prove that, she is still entitled to a divorce provided that she has the means, not to seek divorce in the local court, but to come to the Parliament of Canada, because Parliament 2301
has been consistent in recognizing for-many years the right of husband and wife as being equal where adultery is shown.. f do not think this is right when we know of venereal disease and other matters to which it is not necessary for me to direct the attention of the House, the matter having been put clearly by the President of the Council (Mr. Howell) when he introduced his Bill regarding public health.
I should like to place before the House a record of the number of Canadian divorces and, with the permission of the House, I will put on Hansard the entire record, although I will read for the sake of saving time, only the record from 1914.

were returning from overseas, 87 applications were made to the Parliament of Canada for divorces, and so far, that is to the 17th day of June, 48 divorces have been recommended to this House, and the western cases, so I am told by an official of the Senate, have not been pressed owing to the fact that the applicants are hoping

that this divorce court for which I am urging may be established.
Judicial divorce exists in practically 'every country in the world, with the exception of Italy, Spain and Ireland, and the season divorce courts do not exist there is easily understood. These are, substantially speaking, Roman Catholic countries, and Roman Catholics, as I said at the inception of my remarks, recognize marriage as a sacrament and hold that it cannot be dissolved! It would, therefore, be inconsistent on the part of the people of those countries, staunch as they are to their Church, to establish a divorce court when they are not prepared to recognize that marriage may be dissolved. I may say in passing that Newfoundland has not a divorce court. 'In some countries, there is equality as between the sexes; in others divorce is [DOT] granted to the wife only when she can prove adultery combined with aggravation. In practically every country in the world, when there is a divorce procedure of any sort, adultery is recognized as the ground on which divorce may be obtained.
I have endeavoured to place before this House the history of divorce not only in Great Britain but in Canada as well. I have endeavoured to show how subsequent to the Reformation the Protestant population, cribbed, cabined and confined by the ecclesiastical courts, sought relief from unhappy marriages by an appeal to Parliament, and how that appeal was successful, and subsequently became engrafted on our parliamentary system. I have endeavoured to show how the legislative forum was found to be iso thoroughly unsatisfactory that scandals resulted and the British Isles found iit necessary to constitute a divorce court. It is not difficult for him who runs to read that exactly the same thing that took place in Great Britain has taken, and is taking place in Canada. Parliamentary procedure became necessary in Canada when there was no legal forum to which an appeal could be made, and it is becoming absolutely obvious to him who cares to give the matter consideration that the number of divorce applications that are being made to this Parliament is becoming so great that it is impossible for any member to carry out his parliamentary duties and sit on these cases and give them consideration in a judicial and fair-minded manner. Interested as I was in this subject I endeavoured this year to keep apace with the printed memoranda that came to me from time to time from ithe Senate, but it was

no time at all until I found myself absolutely swamped. It is quite true that I could read in a cursory way what came to me, but I could not value the evidence and weigh the facts as a man should when he sits as a judge on a case, and I submit that every member of this House who gives a vote or silently refrains from voting while a marriage is dissolved in this House takes a responsibility either by his silence or by his vote. So far as I personally am concerned I frankly admit that if parliamentary divorce proceedings are to continue in this House it is going to be quite impossible for me to discharge my duties as I believe they should be discharged. No member can weigh the proceedings of eighty divorce cases, weigh the facts, balance the degrees of probability, and give a decision as a judge, and at the same time attend to his other parliamentary duties.
The interests of the country to-day demand that something be done to facilitate divorce. We must view facts as they are. The conditions in Canada to-day are not a theory; they are facts, they are something every man knows unless, ostrich-like, he hides his head in the sand and is blind to what is taking place. I know, not one, but a dozen, yes fifty cases, and I am satisfied if I made inquiries I could find hundreds of cases, in which men are coming back to Canada and finding, unfortunately, that their wives have not conducted themselves as they should have when the men were away. The Patriotic Fund knows what has been going on in Canada, be it said to our shame, by many oP the women since our men went overseas. Only yesterday in this House a representative of one of the western branches of the Great War Veterans' Association handed me a list of members of his association who had returned to Canada to find an illegitimate child in the house from which they had gone, and in one case it was an illegitimate child of a Chinese laundryman in the district in which the woman lived.
What are these men to do? What is society to do? Are we to force these women to live improperly with the men with whom they have taken up and bring into Canada a brood of illegitimate children? Or are you going to try to force the true husbands to go back to the wives who conducted themselves improperly? If you do not force the men to go badk to the wives that conducted themselves improperly, and I am satisfied that in a great majority of cases they will not go back, you are going to have more common law marriages in this

country than you have any idea of, be-cause-^we may as well look the facts straight in the face-the men who are now returning . to Canada are demanding that they be given a forum in which they may be able to secure separation from the women, who have not conducted themselves as they should have when the men were overseas. If this demand is not met they will live improperly in many cases with the woman of their choice.
I do not want to put all the blame on the women. There are dozens and dozens of men who went overseas and left Canada married men who are coming back to-day with women with whom they went through a form of marriage in England, and these women coming back with them find that there is a wife in Canada and that they have to live with a man who is not their husband, because they have no other place to go. Conditions in Canada to-day, in my judgment, are so serious that Parliament must do something to relieve the situation. There is no use in shutting our eyes to the facts, because it is facts, and not theories, that we have to face in this country.
There is another class of women. There is the true, loyal, straight woman who stayed here in Canada and never departed a fraction from the true and beaten path, but whose husband is not coming back. He has deserted her and taken up with another woman in England Or France and is staying there, and here this woman is in Canada not knowing which way to turn; she does not know what has become of him. Have the deserted wives no rights? It is not as if we had not recognized divorce in this country. It is not as if it were something that had not found its way into our national life and Parliamentary procedure. We have it as a moral right. We have it in various provinces by judicial right. Is any one prepared to say to the residents of the province of Ontario, which [DOT]sent such a magnificent number of men to the front, that the soldier men and the wives of the soldier men in Ontario shall not be entitled to a divorce simply because they have not got $600 or $700, as the case may be, to come down here and secure a parliamentary divorce. I have read not one, but I think half a dozen-and I do not know how many more there are-of the proceedings of the Senate Committee on Divorce this year, in which the fees were rebated because the soldier or the woman said: " Every dollar that I have got I have had to put into this thing, and if you insist before my case is heard that I must deposit
the $210 that is necessary I cannot go on," and the Senate, moved by a sense of compassion and of righteousness, has rebated the fees, or a very substantial part of them, in a number of cases. But the rebate does not cover the entire situation. It has been clearly shown in the proceedings before the Senate this year-and if any gentleman cares to follow this point up he can do so by looking through the divorce cases that have been sent to him-that the parliamentary agent gets $75 for his services, witr nesses have to be brought tens, and in some cases hundreds, if not thousands of miles, with all the incidental expenses, and the application for the proceeding has to be advertised in the Canada Gazette and in two or three papers, as the case may be, in the locality. All this mounts up, and the evidence goes to show that the expense of securing a Senate divorce is in the neighbourhood of from $350 to $750, and sometimes more, depending upon the number of witnesses required and the intensity with which the case is fought.
The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Griesbach) directs my attention to the fact that this varies very much according to distances, and the further people have to come the greater the expense. This means that there is a territorial disadvantage to those who live far from Ottawa. It means a tremendous territorial disadvantage to every woman in the western provinces who cannot get her divorce in western courts unless she can show adultery with aggravation. She must come to Ottawa. If she has been an adulteress and her husband cares to prosecute a divorce against her he can get a divorce in the western court, she on her part cannot get it, because the English law does not recognize adultery without aggravation as being a ground for divorce. It is an anomaly that we cannot allow to continue in this country. Women's societies from the Atlantic to the Pacific are alive to the fact, and they are petitioning for redress; and I do not think that there is a man in the House with any spirit of chivalry who will not recognize the correctness of their position.
The member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) asks me the question:	Can provincial laws be amended by the provincial legislatures? No. Marriage and divorce, by the British North America Act, is restricted to the Dominion Parliament. The only parliament that can amend these provincial laws is the Dominion Parliament, and when an effort has been made in times past to amend them it has not been sue-

cessful in this House. If my memory serves me correctly, Sir John Macdonald at one time tried to secure the appointment of a judge to carry on certain divorce work in the province of New Brunswick and the House would not vote for it because certain members, for conscientious reasons, felt they would be indirectly facilitating divorce if they created machinery by which divorces might be obtained. The net result of it was this: Old, inapplicable, inelastic laws must continue to exist unless this Parliament takes action in the matter. Either it will create a nation-wide divorce tribunal with plenary jurisdiction and equality of law, or it will permit to continue to exist the patch work judicial and parliamentary practice that prevails at the present time.
Now, Sir, I am not going to say for a moment that the Senate have not honestly endeavoured to grapple with the situation. Their rules are very clear. They state that provided certain requirements are met the Committee of- the Senate 'are, with all reasonable despatch to hear and inquire into matters set forth in the petition, and shall take evidence upon oath touching the right of the petitioner to the relief prayed for. I admit that the technical procedure in the Senate is good; and while I do not wish to be considered unduly critical, it seems to me, without criticising that august body, that they have been unduly driven with the applications that come before them. I, a member of Parliament, have been driven this year in endeavouring to keep pace with the printed proceedings as they have come before me, and as every hon. gentleman will understand, it takes longer for the Senate to hear evidence than for u member to read it. And they have been so driven that divorces are being granted on -evidence on which I would not convict a man, if it were equally strong in relation to the facts, in a case of drunkenness. If my wife wanted to get a divorce from me and I were willing to assist her in obtaining it, I do not know of any country in the world, nor do I know of any procedure, in ydiich it can be more easily obtained than in this Parliament. You ask why? The reason is this. The applicant comes to the Senate and puts before the Senate Committee and generally without any sharp or conclusive cross-examination, the alleged facts as set out. As a rule one question is asked the applicant: Has there been any collusion, connivance, or condonation? I have explained what these terms mean. The applicant says, no. Now let me explain why it is easy for a wife to get a 
divorce from her husband. If a man wanted to facilitate his wife obtaining a divorce from him he would tell her: You have to tell one lie to the Clerk of the Senate. He will ask you: Has there been any collusion, connivance or condonation, and you will say, no. If you are prepared to tell that one lie I shall proceed to manufacture the evidence of adultery although I shall never commit it. I shall proceed to obtain some young woman, through a detective agency or otherwise, who will be prepared to lend herself, for a consideration, to the fraud. I shall say to the detective agent: At a certain time tonight I am going to be in a certain hotel. I am first going to a theatre, and then I shall take the young lady to some well known and fashionable restaurant and I want you to be there and see me with her and identify me and the lady. I shall then take her to some place of which I shall inform him, where I shall obtain a room. I shall say to him: We shall register at that hotel as Mr. and Mrs. Doe and you will call me up on the telephone and I shall answer. You will ask for Mrs. Doe and I shall have the young lady go to the telephone, and you will swear there was a lady in the room with me when you go before the Senate /Committee, and to make the adventure absolutely certain the next morning you will come to the room and rap at the -door and I shall arrange that you will see both of us clothed in such costume that the natural inference will be that we had been conducting ourselves not as persons should. You will go before the Senate Committee and swear to that and if necessary I will get confirming evidence by others who are prepared to support me in the fraud. The evidence would be taken with all due dignity and recorded in the proceedings, and our natural conduct would be presumed from the circumstances. In due time there would come into the House a recommendation that the marriage of John Doe and his wife should be dissolved, and that the said John Doe and his wife should be free to marry again. Now, Sir, do we want that kind of thing to go on, or do we want a judicial proceeding established by which there will be a thorough inquiry and examination of all the evidence submitted in divorce cases.
I have told you that I at least am doing my -duty as I see it, in coming to Parliament and saying that I for one cannot discharge my duty and sit as a judge on these cases and I am asking this House to place the proceedings before the courts, and that simply means the creation of a court for the pro-

vince of Ontario and a court for Quebec and unifying the procedure throughout the provinces. By the British North America Act if you pass the Bill to which I am asking this House to give support the divorce courts in the various provinces will be abolished and the new court will be established.
I wish to direct the attention of the House to another aspect of this subject, and that is the political and petticoat influence that is often brought to bear in the endeavour either to secure or to prevent the obtaining of divorces. You get a strenuously contested case before Parliament and there is not one of us who has not seen an attractive applicant or an attractive respondent, if she desired not to have the marriage ties dissolved, not by herself alone but sometimes by equally attractive friends endeavouring to make personal influence a factor in the determination of the case. There have been times when I have known the subtle breezes of political influence to blow in and have seen its effect. There should be nothing of that sort in relation to divorce which should be a judicial proceeding. The facts should be weighed and the rights of parties respected and nothing should be done that would not bear the closest scrutiny and entitle a man to say that the decision was given on the merits of the case regardless of extraneous circumstances.
I do not know whether or not what I have said will impress members, their experience probably will, but I would like to read to them as a sustaining statement something that Lord Brougham said in one of his speeches in reference to the position of divorce in England. He said:
It is certain that no inquiry can be more proper for a, court of law or less adapted to a chamber of Parliament than that of the facts which should entitle parties to divorce.
That puts the matter succinctly, puts it fairly before this Parliament, and I appeal to gentlemen on the other side of the House, and on this side as well, whose religious tenets and whose conscientious beliefs will at least not permit them to vote for the establishment of a divorce court, who resent the establishment within Ontario and Quebec of a divorce court, or who, if they do not resent it, do not desire it-to stand aside at least and let us, whose religious beliefs are not on all fours, with theirs, do something to clarify a domestic and social conuition that is bound to bring distress and sorrow to many homes in Canada.
The desire is not to make divorce easy in the sense that the Bill is creating new
causes or new reasons for which divorce may be had. It is not the time now to go fully into the details of the measure; yet the fundamental principle that governs the Bill is the recognition of the supreme courts in each of the provinces and the establishment of a general court for the Dominion by the vesting of power in the Exchequer Court. Let each court lay down its own procedure, let each court have its rules of practice, but tie it down so that it can only grant a divorce of the marriage tie for adultery or bigamy. The only reason for adding 'bigamy to adultery is that adultery is very often difficult to prove. You have got to hire detectives, prove identification and a thousand and one things. You may grant a divorce for bigamy because any one would naturally accept the proposition that if a man had married a wife the tendency would be towards the consummation of the marriage and by implication it would be said that where a man had gone through, or contracted, a bigamous marriage, the implication of	an	adulterous	relationshipexisted. In this way divorce may be secured, but the causes will not be increased or the procedure widened. I doubt if there are many members of this House who realize the change that has taken place in the practice of	this House,	or,	ratherI might say the enlargement of the Parliamentary practice. Until this year it was a rare thing for a marriage to be annulled on account of impotency. But two cases have gone through, I understand, this year. I	do	not set this	out	in anycritical spirit	but	I speak; of it	as a	lawyer.
I would like every lawyer in this House to read the evidence in those cases. I do not believe any lawyer sitting on either side of this House would have granted a divorce in the Sherk case on the ground of impotency as it was proven. There is another case-Hawkins-where the evidence is no better. That is a case this year I do not know whether or not it has passed this House-but I think it has-where a divorce was granted, the respondent not being present, evidence of the adultery being given by the housekeeper of a house of ill-fame who swore that some six or seven years ago she saw a man whom she alleged was the original of a photograph that was produced to her in a position from which it might reasonably be presumed that he had committed, or was about to commit, adultery. Is there a lawyer in this House who would commit a man on the charge of theft on the ground that some body said that he identified the man because he had seen

him six or seven years ago and there was produced for identification a photograph? That is what it is coming to-indeed, that is what it has come to-'because this House is not the tribunal which should act. If conditions are bad to-day they are going to be worse to-morrow. Are we going to stand by and allow conditions to grow worse until there is a national scandal simply because we have not the courage to handle the situation?
The conditions to-day are not fair. Parliament has recognized the moral right to a divorce being granted. When a man who has the money can come to this House, prove adultery and get his divorce, is ft. fair that those who went overseas should be deprived of this right because they do [DOT] not happen to have the $300 or $400, as the case may be, which may be necessary to get through a Bill? Is divorce to be the rich man's luxury? I am not going to say for one moment that if we had no divorce in Canada some members could not with reason say we are going to keep this thing out of our national life; but are the men who have conscientious objections against this thing, are the men whose religious convictions will not permit them to vote for this Bill, going to vote against it and allow a worse condition to exist than would be the case if this Bill were allowed to pass?
I cannot believe it possible. Members may object on the ground of conscientious scruples, object on the ground of religious convictions, but they should maintain the morals of the Canadian people and maintain a high plane in the national life. I believe this will best be done by the Bill which is now before the House securing the consent of a majority of the members of the House and I am satisfied that if the matter is given fair and due consideration., freed from extraneous or irrelevant objections, the consent I am asking for will be obtained.
