speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise only to thank the hon. membef for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) for the splendid presentation of the case he has given and to place myself on record as supporting the Bill.

subtopic: SECOND BEADING OF DIVORCE BILE MOVED BY MR. NICKL.E.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I have listened with a great deal of attention to the speech made by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) but I must say he has not convinced me that it would be a wise thing for the House to pass this legislation. On the contrary, I am convinced that it would be very dangerous
[Mr. Nickle.[
to pass a Bill that would place the marriage contract and all that it involves upon the same footing as any ordinary contract or dispute to be disposed of by our courts of justice. I have had a great deal of experience in our courts and I regret to say that the respect that was formerly held for the administration of justice is not increasing nor is the oath which is taken by litigants considered with the same solemnity as. it was some years ago. If you open the door to granting divorce I venture to say you will increase the crime of perjury to a great extent.
The argument, as I understood the hon. member, really resolves itself into this: He quotes practically the case of the returned soldiers as a reason why we should depart from the practice that- at present prevails. What is the remedy for that? There is a remedy under the present procedure for people of small means. It is not the case that divorce, under the present system, can only be secured by a person who has a long purse. I have seen cases this session in which the Senate have remitted the fees so as to put divorce within the reach of any person who can .go to any court.
This Bill provides, as I understand it, for an appeal to the Court of Appeal of this province from the decision of a judge sitting nisi prius.. Why an appeal of that kind to the Court of Appeal in the province of Ontario, and probably a further appeal to the Supreme Court, would exceed a thousand dollars. So that the ground of expense does not seem to me to be sufficient ground for opening a door. Make divorces easy to obtain and you will multiply them, I venture to say, in the next five years, by a thousand. Do we want to have in the Dominion of Canada the same condition of affairs that exists in the United States? If there is one thing that Canada and Canadians ought to be proud of, I think it is the respect for the marriage tie which is displayed in this country, and the difficulty there is in getting that tie dissolved. I, for one, Mr. Speaker, would hesitate to depart from the practice that now prevails. Every hon. gentleman in this House who practices law must have hundreds of people coming to him each year, wives or husbands, with difficult matrimonial matters and asking "Cannot we get a divorce?" I say to such people: "No, you can only get a divorce by going to the high court of Parliament. It is a very expensive proceeding, you will have to make out a very strong case," and the result is that these people go home and

make the best of their married life as they promised when they entered into the matrimonial state-for better and for worse. If you make it easy to get a divorce, if you say to any person who consults you: "Yes, we will bring an action to dissolve this marriage, or we will bring an action for divorce," I venture to say that nine-tenths of the litigation before our courts within the next few years will be composed of divorce cases. Hundreds of people consult me about their troubles at home. When you explain to them the present difficulty of getting a divorce, they are perfectly satisfied, and I never hear any more of them. I fancy they return home and by the exercise of a little forbearance are able to live together as man and wife should. If you make it easy for them-and we have unscrupulous practitioners in the legal profession as well as in other businesses-if you put it in the power of solicitors to inaugurate these actions, then, Sir, we will find that the state, of this country would be practically the state of the United States so far as the dissolution of the marriage tie is concerned. Holding these views, I propose to move, seconded by the hon. member for Kings, P.E.I., (Mr. Melsaac):
That this Bill be now not read but that it be read a second time this day six months.

subtopic: SECOND BEADING OF DIVORCE BILE MOVED BY MR. NICKL.E.
speechtext:
I come from a province in which a divorce court has existed ever since 'Confederation, and I think the view which the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) has expressed would 'be very much modified had he ever lived in a province and under a jurisprudence in which divorces were granted by the courts and not by Parliament. The hon. member for Ottawa put his finger upon the real point in issue when he said that it is a question of practice, that is to say, of procedure. This is precisely the question which the House must consider this afternoon.' We are granting divorces in Canada in respect of every province within it at the1 present time. No one has any doubt of that, no one can for a moment question that fact.
It is not a question of establishing any new principle. It is purely a question as to the procedure by which and of the conditions and safeguards under which divorces shall be granted. Can any one believe that so important a matter intimately affecting the social life of our people should be decided under loose procedure by a Parliamentary Committee of the Senate and afterwards by a Committee of the House of Commons rather than in a Court of Justice under all the safeguards which are provided under the practice of courts which deal with such matters?
What is the practice in divorce courts whether in this country or in Great Britain?
It is the practice to provide every possible safeguard and to take every possible precaution that no divorce shall be granted without absolutely satisfactory evidence. It is the practice to provide every possible safeguard against collusion. How is that carried out? By the appointment of a King's Proctor, as he is termed, an able lawyer selected by the court, who is charged with the duty of representing the court and the public interest, who has the right to cross-examine every witness and to address the court and who has the right also to call witnesses in case he suspects the bona fides of the application, the character of the evidence or the probability of collusion.
Compare such practice and such safeguards with the course which prevails in this Parliament, of which I have known something for more than twenty-three years. My hon. friend (Mr. Fripp) truly declares that the question involved in this Bill is one of procedure and of practice; but if he will compare the practice of the courts, the safeguards there provided, with the practice which prevails in the Committees of the Senate and of this House, he will invite at once the defeat of his motion.
I am not desirous of making divorce easy, and I venture to say that the experience of every province in Canada which has a divorce court indicates that the safeguards which are thrown about these applications do not lend themselves to easy divorce. I would challenge any statement to the contrary, because I know-at least I knew very well up to 15 or 20 years ago when I was engaged in the active practice of my profession-the record of the province of Nova Scotia, and the number of divorces up to that period was not large. Contrasted with the record of this Parliament it would, I think, compare very favourably.
Then, so far as is concerned the question of cost; I have been told of witnesses being brought from as far as Edmonton during this very session for the purpose of giving their testimony before the Divorce Committee of the Senate. If we are to grant divorces in Canada, does any good reason exist why that evidence should not be given in the city of Edmonton, or in the city of Calgary, or before some court there under the safeguards that I have mentioned, instead of having these witnesses brought eighteen hundred or two thousand miles to the city of Ottawa that they may give their evi-

dence here. If it is a question of practice, as my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) has said, then,- as far as I am concerned, the practice of placing this question under the safeguards of a court and committing applications for divorce to tribunals which are convenient to the people who may unfortunately be obliged to resort to them, is [DOT]an infinitely better practice than that which we now have in Canada. Therefore, for the reasons which have been very cogently and clearly stated by the hon. member for Kingston, I am in favour of the Bill, the [DOT]second reading of which he now asks the House to approve.
I do not commit myself to every detdil of the Bill because I have not studied it; 1 am dealing only with the general question whether divorces in Canada ought to be granted under proper safeguards by the duly constituted courts of the country or whether they ought to be dealt with by a committee of the Senate and, in a perfunctory way, by a committee of the House of Commons, and without the safeguards which are always available for the trial of *causes in the courts of this country.

subtopic: SECOND BEADING OF DIVORCE BILE MOVED BY MR. NICKL.E.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with a view to obtaining certain information that was necessary for the Canadian Patriotic Fund in determining whether there was a field of usefulness for it after the war, I circularized all the principal branches throughout Canada to .find out whether, if the fund should .suddenly terminate, there would be any considerable number of residual cases, that is, eases of women and children who would be left without any means of support and who would not be provided for by the military pension, or other allowances. I asked our branches to state in all cases what were the reasons why certain families now on the fund would be without means [DOT]of support if the fund should terminate.
I was surprised to find in looking over the returns we got them from every part of Canada, long lists of cases of women and children in distress-that a very considerable number of them were deserted wives of men who had gone overseas; the wives of men who had been married overseas or of men who, having gone overseas, had discovered wives that they had previously had over there and remained with them. There was no means by which these families could be helped except through the Patriotic Fund, and I realized what the people of this country do not realize: That when a woman permitted her hus-
band to enlist and go overseas, she ran not two risks, but three. She ran, first, the risk that he would be killed and she would be a widow; in which case she would undoubtedly be adequately provided for by way of pension by a grateful country. She ran the second risk that her husband would be seriously maimed or injured and that she would have to live with a cripple for the remainder of her life. The Government recognizes that contingency under the pension law and will undoubtedly meet it in the future. But no one has realized the third contingency: That when a woman lets her husband go overseas and be absent a number of years, conditions might arise, aside from casualty, under which he might not come back; and there are a great many women in Canada to whom that third condition has come.
I want to put in a plea for these women, many of whom are without children, some of whom have one, two, or three young children. I want to put in a plea that it be made possible for them to begin life again under new and better circumstances. These women, for the most part, are poor; they cannot earn any considerable sums of money. The obtaining of the three or four hundred dollars necessary to enable them to come to Ottawa and get a divorce is as impossible to them as the raising of enough money to build a Parliament building. It is impossible for them to secure any form of relief. Are you going to ask these women to live the remainder of their lives neither married or unmarried? They have to look after themselves, and if you do nothing for them in this connection you put them in a position where they are likely to fall and to increase that portion of the population which we consider undesirable. If you establish divorce courts in the various provinces, in cases of this kind distressed wives may, without great expense, appear before them and prove desertion without difficulty by producing letters from their husbands showing that they are living with other women; and in this way you will make it possible for them to secure relief. You will make it possible for a woman so situated to begin life again, to re-marry under happier circumstances, to open 'another home, perhaps, in some western portion of Canada where she and her children may live an honourable and a-happy life. In view of the special war conditions that have arisen and of this special consideration which was not with us before, we must face facts as they are; and I submit this argument to the House as one of the reasons why legislation

of the character suggested should be passed, and passed now.
Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queens) Mr. Speaker, the member for Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) in strongly opposing this measure, said that if it should pass, the cases of divorce would be multiplied by thousands. If his statement is well founded -and I know it is his deliberate judgment -then that which he regards as a reason for the rejection of this Bill is the strongest possible argument in its favour. If thousands of honest men and women in this country are entitled to divorce, not on new grounds-as the member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) has shown, we are not introducing new grounds-not on trifling grounds such as, we are told, divorces are granted in some other countries, but upon the well-established grounds recognized by our courts and by this Parliament, the fact that these men and women are entitled to divorce and are unable to get it because of the present machinery is the strongest argument why that machinery should be discarded and some better machinery set up.
There are strong religious objections to divorce. The most numerous religious body iti this country is known to have strong objections to divorce, and another very considerable religious body has, to some degree, similar objections. These objections, which are based upon religious grounds, are entitled to our most profound respect, and if they succeeded in preventing divorce then we might by all means commend them. But they do not do anything of the sort. We are not considering to-day the question whether or not divorce shall be granted. Divorce is granted in some of the provinces, as has been shown, by judicial machinery, and at Ottawa by machinery which cannot be called judicial and to which you can hardly properly apply any term of respect. Divorce, therefore, is being granted and is going to be granted; the only question is whether it shall be granted by decent machinery, or by that which is a burlesque of justice. That is the whole question. If any hon. member thinks that he can prevent the granting of divorce by opposing this Bill I understand his position and respect him for it. But since divorce is going to be granted anyhow, and since the only question is whether it is to be granted in the decent way described by the Prime Minister when he referred to the method pursued in the province from which we both come surely there should be no hesitation. I very cordially support the member for Kingston.

subtopic: SECOND BEADING OF DIVORCE BILE MOVED BY MR. NICKL.E.
speechtext:
It does not appear to me that this Bill is one which this House should pass. It may be quite true it is the better method of conducting divorce proceedings, but one of the first things that struck me when I went overseas a few years ago was the ease with which divorces were granted in the old country. It did not seem to my mind to lend any dignity to either the judicial proceedings or to the nation. It looked very much as though it were a case if a man wanted to get a divorce from his wife, that practically all he had to do was to spend a night with a certain party, notify his wife of the fact and tell her to get a divorce, which probably she proceeded to do. It acted, of course, in the reverse way as well. I think when we compare conditions in this country, bad and all as they may be, with conditions in the United States or Great Britain where divorces are undoubtedly made easier, all credit will stand in favour of Canada. The marriage tie is a

question which should not be made a football. People should not enter into a contract of that kind without serious consideration, without estimating all the consequences, and this Parliament should hesitate before placing this country in a similar position to that which may exist in such places as the American Republic and even in Great Britain. Such a course does not add to the dignity of the nation, nor to the dignity of Parliament.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. M. M. TWEEDIE (Calgary West):
subtopic: SECOND BEADING OF DIVORCE BILE MOVED BY MR. NICKL.E.
speechtext:
I wish to say just a few words in support of this Bill. I have been somewhat surprised at the line of argument in the speeches of the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) and one or two others. They would lead us to believe that divorce .when procured before the Senate is, in all cases, founded upon fraud and corruption, and that if applicants go to the courts and the jurisdiction is transferred, we are still going to have fraud and corruption there. There is no distinction whatever between divorce evidence and any other evidence, and it is only fair to assume that the people who are applying for divorce, no matter what the forum may be, are entitled to be credited with being as honest as any other citizens. It is true there may be some fraud or some corruption, but the question is: Should divorce be granted in the Pominion of Canada at all? I am absolutely of the opinion that it should be. I cannot conceive of any law which should compel a man to be tied to a woman, or a woman to be' tied to a man for the rest of their natural days, when either one of the parties is living openly in adultery or has committed bigamy. That is all this Bill provides for; it confines the grounds upon which divorce may be granted to those simple grounds, and as the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) fears that divorces may become common in this country and may be easy, if he will read the report of the commission to the Imperial Government, which commission reported prior to the war, he will find there what will be practically a revelation to him as to what, in their opinion, may be considered as grounds for divorce. We do not wish to extend the jurisdiction; we wish simply to transfer the place where the case may be heard, and it is absolutely unfair, as it has been in the past, that any person should be compelled to come from Alberta and bring his witnesses with him and, in some cases, his counsel and incur expendi-

ture of anywhere from $2,000 to $5,000 before securing a divorce. If a divorce is good for the man who has the means, it is absolutely as good for the man who has not, and money, that is, the ability to supply the necessary funds to defray the costs, should not be the test; the test should be the two principles that are set down in this Bill, that either party is chargeable with adultery or bigamy. The jurisdiction of Alberta has not yet been determined, but it will be determined by the Privy Council. I do not think, however, we need wait for that. If any doubt exists at the present time, in my opinion, it is the duty of this Parliament, as regards that province and indeed all other provinces, to remove that doubt. There should be uniformity. Why should the divorce court in Nova Scotia or the Supreme Court in British Columbia have jurisdiction over marriages and be able to grant divorces, while the interior provinces are denied that privilege? If, as the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) points out, those courts can administer that branch of the law satisfactorily, that privilege can safely be extended to the other provinces to which it has been denied in the past. This is one of the best pieces of legislation which has been introduced into this House at this session, and I trust the majority of the members will see their way clear to give their support to the hon. member for Kingston.

subtopic: SECOND BEADING OF DIVORCE BILE MOVED BY MR. NICKL.E.
speechtext:
I am very glad that the hon. member for Kingston has brought in this Bill. I have nothing further to add to the excellent reasons he has given in favour of it than perhaps to mention two conditions which pertain to soldiers particularly and also to the West. For the last year or so, I do not think a week has passed but I have had soldiers in my office at Calvary who have furnished me with sufficient evidence to make it perfectly clear that they are entitled to a divorce, but I have had to tell them that it will cost them .possibly about $2,000 to get that divorce, when they consider the number of witnesses they have to bring from that point, their hotel expenses here and possibly the necessity of making another trip to Ottawa, because sometimes divorces have been only partly heard when Parliament has prorogued and the witnesses have had to return to their homes and to come back the next year. When I told them that, it became perfectly apparent that those men could not get a divorce. Divorce should not be a luxury

only for the rich; it should be open to the poor, and on that broad ground I wish to give the Bill my support. I have had soldiers say to me such things as this: We have gone overseas to fight for our country; we have come back; we cannot get our rights here, and we will go to the United States, where we can get our rights. I have known of several cases where soldiers have gone to the United States to get their rights.
As regards the question of uniformity, even if the Privy Council decides that Alberta has power under the old English jurisdiction to grant divorces, that divorce will still have that fault mentioned by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), namely, the fact that the wife, in order to get a divorce, must show additional aggravation, and I do not think we desire that to have any part in our divorce law in Alberta. For these reasons I shall support the Bill.

subtopic: SECOND BEADING OF DIVORCE BILE MOVED BY MR. NICKL.E.
speechtext:
A few years ago I would have been inclined to oppose this Bill, but during the last four years I have had the honour of being chairman of the Private Bills Committee, before which the divorce Bills come, and with other hon. gentlemen I have had the privilege of attending, by arrangement, the Senate Committee on Divorce. I must confess that my attendance there has entirely changed my views on the existing procedure for granting divorce in Canada. In the light of that expei'ience I am prepared to support the Bill introduced by the hon.. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle). I think the House is unanimous in desiring to prevent any pulling down of the bars in the granting of divorce. I quite appreciate all the arguments that have been put forward as to the necessity for keeping the expense of securing a divorce down to such a figure that the poor applicant will be able to secure one as well as the rich.
I shall support the Bill, not only because it may reduce the expense of securing a divorce, but because I believe that we should make it as difficult as possible, when the case is actually being tried, for the applicant to secure the divorce, and no divorce should be granted unless evidence is produced that absolutely proves the charges.
Under our present system the greatest evil is not the cost because after all the only essential cost so far as the Committee of Parliament is concerned is a matter of $210, all the other costs being incurred through the employment of counsel and travelling expenses; the great evil is that under the present system divorces can be obtained, and are being obtained, on evidence which, as the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) has said, would not be accepted by the judge of any court in the land. I have seen several divorces granted during the present year which no judge or lawyer entrusted with the examination of witnesses would have been disposed to grant for one moment. I therefore think that the change in the procedure that is proposed will reduce, rather than increase, the number of divorces, and that is the reason I am supporting the Bill.

What is the object oi having the Exchequer Court, as well as the provincial courts, charged with this function?
It was thought that while a court should be constituted for each province it might also be well to have one Dominion court with co-ordinate jurisdiction in reference to divorce.
Then you will have two courts. An applicant for divorce may choose whether he shall go to the provincial court or to the Exchequer Court.

With this difference, that any person domiciled in Canada would have the right to go to the Exchequer Court, but any person domiciled in one of the provinces must confine his application w the court of that province.

To be domiciled in
Canada one must be domiciled in one of the provinces of Canada or in the Yukon territory. What is the difference? It looks to me like creating two courts for the same purpose.

For instance, in the event of a divorce being sought, possibly in the province of Quebec/ and the judiciary being at any time of the Roman Catholic faith and having conscientious objections to granting divorce, they might find themselves in a most embarrassing and difficult position providing they bad to consider an application for divorce and give a decision, and I thought it unfair to put them in such a position.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I had intended raising the same objection that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) has made. I do not quite appreciate the necessity of vesting jurisdiction in the Exchequer Court of Canada, for the very reason that the hon. gentleman has advanced. The practice in the courts of the different provinces is quite different from the practice in the Exchequer Court, and usually in the latter case is much more expensive, although I do not know whether that would hold good with respect to divorce cases. Unless there is some good reason for it, I certainly would urge upon the hon. gentleman who is promoting this Bill to reconsider the question.

I felt very much impressed by the necessity of avoiding anything that might bring embarrassment to any judge. I have a high regard for people's conscientious objections and religious beliefs, and to avoid the possibility of causing offence I thought there could be no objection to giving the Exchequer Court jurisdiction in these cases. I trust the leader of the Opposition will concur in that idea,' although he may be of the opinion that Exchequer Court jurisdiction is unnecessary at the present time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My objection is based on the reason advanced by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding), that we are duplicating the courts. It is true that at present, as regards the provinces, some cases can go to the County Courts and also to the Supreme Court. There is concurrent jurisdiction, but those cases are all in the one province. As I understand the Exchequer Court procedure, the Attorney

General, representing the Crown, can start an action without a fiat, and anybody else desirous of instituting proceedings has to get a fiat from the Government, and there is a lot of preliminary difficulty in regard to it that is foreign to the issue of a writ in the ordinary courts. If the necessity does not exist, I think it is rather undesirable to be multiplying difficulties.

The explanation made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Nickle) brings to my mind another set of cases that might arise under the proposal to give jurisdiction to the Exchequer Court. The very fact that it is more difficult to enter an action in that court, and perhaps more expensive, may lead to cases where the applicant for divorce will purposely choose the Exchequer Court in order to involve the respondent in financial or other difficulties. For instance, an action might be brought in the Exchequer Court where the respondent lived in British Columbia and the applicant in Quebec. This would put the respondent to a great deal of expense and trouble, and not only that, but it would, perhaps, lead to a divorce going through which might not be granted in the provincial courts.

I would hardly imagine such a situation as that would arise, for the reason that the Exchequer Court moves from place to place; it has no fixed location from which its decisions are given; and in the determination of the place at which the trial should - be held consideration would have to be given to the request and the position of the applicant, and others, and no doubt the question would be settled on motion.
Mr. BUREAU. There are only two judges of the Exchequer Court. Suppose the senior judge should die; the assistant judge is a Roman Catholic, and until a successor was appointed the condition would not be as it is in Quebec, where a great many of the judges are not Roman Catholics.

I suggest that we go through these relationships seriatim; as the hon. gentleman has read them, they are nothing but a Babel of confusion.

Of course, it is most confusing. Really this provision was the adoption in the time of Henry VJII of the canonical law in reference to consanguinity and affinity. Did I hear the words "sister-in-law" read in the schedule? If I mistake not, I have seen something like this in the English Church prayer book. If that is in the schedule, would not a deceased wife's sister be a sister-in-law?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I know of a case where a man married his brother's widow. I certainly did not approve of it; I thought it was not a proper thing to do from a moral standpoint, but I did not know it was against the law because we have no Statute on that point in any province so far as I know.
We have in Quebec.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In Nova Scotia, we have no Statute on that point. We would regard it as being common law with us according to the law of Henry VIII.

Is there not something in this that might be an encroachment upon the rights of the provinces? According to the British North America Act, matters concerning marriage and



divorce come under the Federal authorities, but on the other hand, in the following clause, it is stated that all things pertaining to the solemnization of marriage come under provincial jurisdiction. In some provinces, at least in the province from which I come, there is a law concerning the degrees of relationship that are prohibited. Supposing those provisions should not be the same, shall it be said that a man who is married according to the laws of his province could see his marriage annulled by a law of this Parliament as the one which will be passed now? There might be a conflict. I think the question ought to be studied before we pass this legislation.

I would be inclined to think that "marriage and divorce" as defined in the British North America Act would give the Dominion the right of determining the status of the parties and their right to enter into the state of matrimony. I would hardly like to go the length of saying-and I do not think my hon. friend will so argue-that the relationship of the parties had anything to do with the ceremony incidental to the marriage. If I may use the expression, I would think the status of the parties went to the very heart of the question, whereas the ceremony was more a surface arrangement, to carry my figure through.

I do not pTofess to be an authority on ecclesiastical law, but my recollection is that when the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill was passed in Canada in 1883 -my hon. friend refers to 1907 which was the year the British Act was passed, but we were quite ahead of Great Britain in that respect-the leaving out of the deceased husband's brother was a mere omission. Logically there is no reason why we should not do now what should have been done in 1883, and say that if a man can marry his deceased wife's sister, a woman can marry her deceased husband's brother. They are in the same degree of consanguinity, and we should not perpetuate the error of 1883.
What is the difference between a marriage which will be dissolved and a marriage which will be declared null and void ?

The distinction lies in this: A marriage is dissolved when a marriage has actually taken place, and a marriage is annulled when it is declared by the court never to have existed. As I endeavoured to explain this afternoon, the word " divorce "
[Mr ,E. Lapointe.]
as commonly used in English jurisprudence is used as applicable not only to a recision but to an annulment. The difference would be this, to give an example: If A and B were married and had children, and if as the result of the misconduct of either, the marriage was dissolved, the children would still be legitimate. If, on the other hand, a man and a woman, although within the kindred degrees prohibited by the Act to which I have just directed attention, had gone through a form of marriage, that marriage would be void ab initio, and the children would not and could not be legitimate. One determines the dissolution of the marriage, determines the separation as from the date of the declaration. The annulment is a declaration of the fact that the marriage never existed and never should have existed in the eyes of the law.
If the issue is illegitimate, that is not right.

It was to get over that point that the proviso was put in:
Provided, however, that no marriage shall be declared null and void after the death of one of the .parties thereto unless such marriage was void ab initio.
But there is no question whatever that the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) is correct in this, that an annulment which dates back to the date of the marriage makes any children subsequently-born illegitimate and illegally bom.

That is the unfairness of the thing. People might have been married in good faith, ignorant of any of the causes which would render the marriage void, and yet the issue would be illegitimate. A provision ought to be inserted which would make children born from that marriage legitimate. Of course, technically -and legally, there never was a marriage, but for all purposes of society, if people have been living together in good faith and find out later on that, on account of a legal technicality, they were not married, the issue should not suffer from that.
My idea in drafting this legislation was'to disturb as little as possible the general law of the land as it has been recognized for generations.
We could improve on that.

This Bill goes further than the hon. gentleman contemplates. As I understand it, it will dissolve a marriage solemnized in the United States or any other country where the parties in question are domiciled in Canada. In the United

States, they have not this law according to Henry VIII, and marriages are celebrated there within much closer degrees of consanguinity than we have in Ontario or any other province. As a matter of fact, the marriage law of Ontario does not go as far as the schedule enumerated by the hon. member (Mr. Nickle). I know it is placed on the back of the application for a marriage license, and I am sure there are not nearly so many degrees of consanguinity mentioned. In certain states in the American Union a man may legally marry his deceased brother's wife. I have in mind at present two cases in which such a marriage has been solemnized and the parties are residents of this country. By this Bill, if it goes through, the children by such a marriage will be illegitimate to all intents and purposes and can be so declared by anybody. We should go. slow in this [DOT]matter, because it certainly involves the rights of innocent parties.

Could not a proviso be inserted to protect the issue in a case like that? My hon. friend says this has always been the law, but even so, that is no reason why, if that law is not just, we should not improve it, if we are going to legislate on the subject.
Mr. NI'CKLE: In reply to the ,hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs), this legislation was, of course, drafted for Canada.
Mr. ARTHUR,S: Does it not dissolve a marriage which has been celebrated in the United States if the parties are domiciled in Canada?
No.
It declares it to be illegal.

No, it says that the Exchequer Court of Canada shall have jurisdiction and may declare the marriage null and void in certain specified cases. I have very grave doubts if a court would declare null and void a marriage that had been solemnized in the United 'States, provided that the parties came to Canada and had a matrimonial domicile in this jurisdiction. I would incline to the view that the court would say: " Having entered into the contract of marriage under regulations in another country that entitle you to marrriage, this court refuses to exercise its discretionary power and relieve you from the contract which you entered into in good faith."

Why not remove all
doubt by placing that in the Bill?
I would ask my hon. friend to reconsider that point; the clause might stand in the meantime.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I voted for the second reading of this Bill in good faith, believing that the only question involved was a better method of enforcing the law as it now stands respecting divorce. I think that what this House desires is that we should provide a better means of enforcing the law as it now stands, but not that we should not in any way disturb the present status of the marriage laws or widen the grounds on which divorce may be granted. The clause we are now dealing with has a very wide scope, and is capable of constructions that might cause a great deal of trouble. I do not profess to understand the full effect of this clause. If I had had time to read the Bill before the second reading I would have strongly urged the hon. member to send the Bill to a special committee, and if there is any way now of having that done, I would suggest that it be done. Very nice and highly technical questions are involved affecting the most sacred relations of the people, and I am afraid that the Committee of the Whole is not the best place in which to deal with this Bill.

I quite appreciate the difficulty of the situation and the nicety of the questions involved, but I doubt very much if I have in any way widened the scope of the law, or extended it in such a way as to make it any broader than the parliamentary practice that now prevails or the practices prevailing in the various courts. Let us analyse for a moment the different grounds on which marriage may be declared null and void. If a marriage is a contract it necessarily carries with it the idea that each of the parties to the contract must give consent,-you cannot have a contract without the parties to that contract being; at some time at one. Let us take the sections as they appear. Paragraph (a) says that any marriage may be declared null and void:
-at the suit of the injured party, or the incurable physical impotence of a .party to a marriage which existed at the time of the marriage.
In my remarks to this House this afternoon I directed attention to the fact that during the present session two marriages have been declared void by Parliament, or are in the process of being so declared, on account of physical impotency. That has been the lav/ in this Parliament and is the law in the various provinces.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I take no exception
to that. That has*always been understood to be the law.
Mr. NI'CKLE:	We come now to paragraph (b) which says that the marriage may be declared null and void.
__for duress, coercion or want of consent at
the suit of the injured party, unless such party has toy his consent confirmed the marriage.
As those in the House who are lawyers know, duress means obtaining consent, I suppose, by force. It simply means that a marriage may be declared null and void where there has been no re-consent, provided that the injured party, that is the party who has had the marriage forced on him or her, is desirous of having the marriage dissolved. It would be radically unfair that a marriage should be declared null and void where there was duress, provided the party forced into the marriage was not desirous of having it dissolved. For instance, in the case of a woman forced into marriage by friends or otherwise, in the event of her having become pregnant it would be radically unjust that the marriage at the suit of the husband should be declared void. She being injured, and having been forced to consent, it might be that she might not be willing to have the marriage terminated, and her father might demand that it be not terminated.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The word " duress,"
so far as I know, does not appear in our Nova Scotia statutes. If a person was forced into marriage it might come under the head of cruelty. Cruelty is a ground for divorce in Nova Scotia, but I think the word " duress " is new.

I think that the idea here was to deal with the cases of very young persons. There is a statute iu Ontario, passed five or six years ago, which provided that the courts should dissolve the marriage of two young persons who are under the age of eighteen, I think it is, provided the marriage has not been consummated, and several applications have been made under that Act. The point raised by my hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) has been discussed in the courts, and one learned judge, Chief Justice Richard Meredith, has very definitely stated that he does not think the statute comes within the powers of the legislature. I think that this Bill would undoubtedly come within the power of this -*parliament. These want of consent cases would be those of persons so young that they are not supposed to have arrived at

the age where they can give consent, and the legislation before us would implement the existing legislation providing that a marriage should be dissolved which had been entered into foolishly and without consideration between two young persons.

I understand that the object of this Bill is simply to give jurisdiction to the various provinces to try divorce cases, instead of those cases coming before the Senate. I think the object of my hon. friend from Kingston, from his point of view, is laudable. It is to avoid the publicity and cut down the expense. Why not enact that divorce cases shall be tried before the courts enumerated in the Bill without changing the grounds for divorce in any respect whatever? I do not know just what the grounds are; I have never closely studied divorce law because, as my hon. friend will understand) we do not touch these cases. But I would suggest that the grounds for divorce which exist to-day should still subsist, and we need simply transfer the jurisdiction from Parliament to the , courts of the different provinces as enumerated in the first section. The whole thing could be done in one clause.

The impracticability of that suggestion will be seen when I draw attention to the fact that in the various provinces divorce may be obtained for different reasons. In Nova Scotia, for instance, I think cruelty is a ground for divorce being granted; in some other province it is desertion, sometimes for a longer and sometimes for a shorter period. But when you apply that principle to Ontario and Quebec it will not work because we have never had in either Ontario or Quebec any law in regard to divorces. It has always been a parliamentary discretion. Parliament is not limited in any way as to reasons for which a divorce may be granted. If Parliament were capricious and decided that two persons might be divorced in the event of both having red hair, if that Bill could be forced through Parliament, the divorce would be illegal, because parliamentary divorces are by way of private bills and they dissolve marriage simply in the case to which reference is made. I therefore had to incorporate in this Bill the general principles of the law as they are and have been recognized up to the present by parliamentary practice and procedure. There is, however, one exception to which I would like to direct the attention of the committee,

and that is section (c) which states that marriage may be declared null and void:
__(e) at the suit of the husband, when the
wife is pregnant at the time of the marriage by a man other than the husband, if the husband was ignorant of the pregnancy at the time of such marriage and has not, after the discovery by him of such pregnancy, by his conduct confirmed such marriage;
That struck me as being an eminently fair reason for which declaration of nullity might be obtained. In the event of a woman having been indiscreet and having reached a condition that demanded marriage to protect her name, if she inveigles some man into unknowingly marrying her and he subsequently discovers that she is pregnant to another man, he is entitled, if he so desires, to have the marriage declared null and void. Directing my attention for a moment again to the remarks of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) and referring to subsection (d) in which power is given to declare the marriage null and void for insanity at the time of the marriage of either of the parties, it still carries out the same principle to which I at first directed attention, that if there was no consent there could be no marriage, because marriage is a contract and if a person is insane he or she is unable to give valid consent. And taking subsection (f) which gives power to the courts to declare marriage null and void at the suit of the injured party, when the other party wilfully refuses to consummate the marriage, these are all a confirmation of principles repeatedly recognized in this Parliament.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I wish to say now, in the presence of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) that I voted for the second reading of the Bill with the understanding that I was affording more complete machinery for enforcing the law as it now stands. If the hon. member for Kingston were able to present to the Committee the various grounds upon which the Senate of Canada had been granting divorces for the last fifty years or so I would feel no difficulty. I am quite willing that we should furnish machinery for the granting of divorces for any cause for which the Senate would grant them. But I am not familiar with any cases of the class last mentioned by the hon. member as having been before the Senate, and I do not think that they grant divorces in cases of that kind. If they do, I would be satisfied, but I am not in favour of widening the scope of grounds for divorce.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have not been present during all the discussion. I am
impressed with the view put forward by the hon. member for Kingston, that if we are to establish courts in those provinces which have none at the present time, and to provide a law in those provinces because no divorce law exists there, it would be an. unfortunate course if we should so frame our law that one ground for divorce would be sufficient in one province and not in another. The principles in that respect would not be uniform. It is necessary not. only to establish courts in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec but also to establish; principles; and if you establish principles there, then you must have regard for the principles which have already been established in the provinces where jurisdiction in divorce exists. The course that has been taken by my hon. friend (Mr. Nickle) is, as I understand, to examine the grounds which prevail in iGreat Britain and in the various provinces, and the jurisdiction that has been exercised, and out of that to bring certain principles here, which certainly do not extend the grounds upon which divorce may be granted in some of those places. The section in that respect is rather restrictive than enabling, and I think that every one of the grounds here, except the one which the hon. member for Kingston has just now alluded to, is regarded as a proper ground either for pronouncing a divorce a vinculo matrimonii, or declaring a marriage null and void ab initio

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Prime Minister
will consider the case of insanity. This is a very insidious disease and exists sometimes for a long time before it can really be pronounced as actual insanity. I do not want to give any excuse to any man to get clear of the responsibilities of the marriage contract. If a .man's wife happens to get out of her mind-oritmaybethe other way about-he will say:	Although I did
not discover it at the time, she was insane when I married her and the contract ought to be set aside. That, I think, would be giving rise to a very grave difficulty and something that is not known in our courts. I have never heard of any attempt being made to set aside marriage because some person has happened to develop insanity, and this principle is capable of creating a great deal of trouble.

I hold in my hand the
Civil Code of Quebec and would direct the attention of the hon. member for Kingston to titles of it, section 115 and the following sections. The hon. member for Kingston has read a schedule he has attached to his Bill, and I think that this schedule

would be in contradiction of section 126 *of the Civil Code of Quebec. If I understand the matter rightly the situation would be this:	A man could apply to a court
in accordance with our federal divorce law and obtain an annulment of his marriage, while, under our Civil law, his marriage would be valid. The consequence would be that although he was divorced from his wife nevertheless, according to our Civil law, she would still have the rights of a wife.

As I said before the hon. member (Mr. Cannon) came into the House, in my opinion marriage and divorce is set out in the British North America Act and jurisdiction is in this Parliament enabling the Dominion House to determine the status of parties and the relationship of each to the other permitting them to marry. If this Act passed, I think the kindred degrees regarded as entitling persons to legally enter matrimony would he those I read to the House as expressed in subsection (c) which I promised to make a schedule.
Mr. MoGIBBON (Muskoka):	Subsection
(d) is absolutely useless unless this Parliament is going to enforce a medical examination of both parties at the time of marriage. No man will take six months, twelve months or two years after the marriage has taken place to know if the party was sane or insane at the time of marriage.

I think the hon. member overlooks the position that the court would take. The Act says that the court may declare the marriage null and void for insanity at the time of the marriage of either of the parties thereto. It will be incumbent upon the person desiring a declaration of nullity to prove to the court that the other party was insane and the principle upon which the decision is generally given is that the onus of proof is on the party making complaint. If the condition is that six months after the marriage it would be impossible to say whether or not the person was insane at the time of marriage, the proof would fail and the marriage would be declared legal.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The difficulty is that once a husband and wife enter the court for the purpose of dissolving their marriage it is an end to all happiness. The * court may refuse a divorce but that does not re-establish happy relations in that family. If a man is encouraged to go into court thinking that he has an insane wife, that is the end of it. He may not succeed in proving that she is insane but it breaks
IMr. Cannon.]
up the family and destroys the confidence that should exist between a man and his wife. My view is that we should confine the reason for divorce to the grounds of immorality. I am not fond of making new contractual relations and that sort of thing. The reason why a marriage would be set aside on the ground of insanity would be the same as the setting aside of a deed or conveyance given by an insane person-because the party signing it was insane when he signed it. This question of insanity is entirely new to me. I cannot bring myself to agree to this provision.

The reason bigamy was put in as well as adultery is this: As I explained in the House this afternoon, it is often most difficult to prove that adultery has taken place. The fact that there is a bigamous marriage is more easily proven. If a man who is already married goes through a form of marriage with a second woman and commits bigamy, it is not unreasonable, but rather natural, to suppose that as a result of that bigamous marriage an adulterous relationship with the second wife will take place.
iMr. E. LAPOINTE: This Bill is more important than some hon. members may realize. It has been introduced by a private member of the House when there is no time for the consideration of private members' business. No one expected that the Bill would be proceeded with this session, and that is a good reason why we have not studied it as it should have been studied before being discussed by the House. I respectfully suggest that the Committee should rise and report progress and that members should have an opportunity of studying the Bill before discussion be proceeded with. The question of provincial rights arises, which is most important. There have been many discussions in this House about the rights of the Dominion and the provinces concerning marriage matters. There is the question of eivil rights which has been raised by my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon). It is only fair that I should ask the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sii Robert Borden) to give us an opportunity of studying the Bill. It is a most important piece of legislation, and I ask that its consideration should be postponed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As far as posh ponement for a reasonable time is concerned, I think the hon. member (Mr. E. Lapointe) is quite within his rights in asking it. I do not like to undertake any engagement further than that. If that is the desire, I shall move that the Committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
