speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. J. A. Calder (Minister of Immigration and Colonization) Bill No. 131 for the promotion of Technical Education in Canada was read a second time, and the House went into Committee thereon-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 2-definition:

Would the minister give an explanation of the words in paragraph (c): under which the various forms of technical education are to be-
-approved by agreement between the minister and the Government of any province as being necessary or desirable to aid in promoting industry and the mechanical trades.
Why is it necessary to have the approval of the minister and the Provincial Government interested? I think it would be better to define in this section what me mean by technical education. I understand the intention of the Bill is to promote technical education and I do not think that the definition as to what it is should be left to any agreement but should be made by law.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
"Technical education'' as used to-day is a somewhat loose term. Sometimes it is used almost synonomously with "vocational education," and we also have the term "industrial education." The purpose of defining the term in this way is, as the paragraph states, to leave the character of the education to be carried on 'to an agreement between the provincial and the federal authorities. Personally, I am inclined to the view that the real purpose of the Bill will be served best by leaving that; as a matter of agreement between the two Governments. Technical education as strictly applied usually refers to the class of work that is carried on in a technical institution, but it seems to me that we must give it a broader meaning. I know the Minister of Labour has in mind the advisability of arranging for a class of education that will be carried on outside of these technical institutions that are provided for in some of the provinces. Probably the term "industrial education" would be more applicable than "technical education." Allow me to give an example. In one of our cities certain industries are established in which there are a large number of employees. It may be advisable to provide means whereby certain classes of instruction can be carried on in those industrial establishments. The idea is to have the widest possible meaning in order that in the provinces concerned the Minister

of Labour may reach an agreement as to the application of the term "technical education" as it is desired to be used in many particular instances.

The definition given in the paragraph seems to be wide enough. It seems to cover everything from teaching a man how to saw wood with a handsaw to imparting instruction in industrial chemistry. Why should the system of instruction proposed under this Bill be determined by special agreement? In 'our province we have a technical school at Three Rivers and one at Shawinigan Falls. At the latter place there are various industries. For instance, the Canadian Chemical Company manufactures chemicals, and they have a branch in which industrial chemistry is taught. Paper is also manufactured there, and instruction in paper-making is given. The manufacture of calcium carbide is also carried on. Each town or centre ought to be able to provide the means to help develop its particular industries. Now, suppose the minister makes an agreement with a province, and in the meantime a new industry should be established as to which some special institution for giving instruction might be needed; in that case, apparently, it would derive no advantage from the money which is to be voted under this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
The idea back of this legislation may be shortly put as follows: The Minister of Education of a province- or whatever provincial minister has the administration of the Act-will, in conjunction with the Minister of Labour, determine the manner in which these moneys are to be supplied for the purpose of technical education within the province. Now it seems to me that if you get down to a restriction of this definition it will only tend to defeat the object of the Bill. My own idea is that the more elastic the provision the safer it will be. The Agricultural Aid Act, as I understand it-I have nothing to do with the administration of the law-has worked out very well indeed. As the hon. gentleman can quite well understand, where we are providing advances for agricultural education and agricultural extension work, there is a great variety of undertakings to which that might be ap-. plied. But the provinces and tne Federal Government have had practically no difficulty in coming to an agreement as to the manner in which those moneys should be expended, and I think there will be very little difficulty in this case, if the law is left as it is.
[Mr. Oalder.l
I think it will be distinctly advantageous to leave the law in such form that the provinces and the Dominion may come to an agreement as to the manner in which the moneys are to be expended. I have not the slightest doubt that the wishes of the province with regard to the application of these moneys will be very largely respected by the federal authorities.

I agree that we should not impose undue restrictions as to the application of the moneys, on the contrary, we should provide that all cases where expenditure of this kind may be desirable shall be covered, and it is just for that reason that I think these things should not be defined or determined in an agreement entered into between the Federal Government and the provincial authorities. Let us set out in the Act the full interpretation and signification of the words " technical education."

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's contention would be sound if an unlimited amount of money was to be applied to this purpose. But the amount is limited, and there must be some selection of the many forms of activity available for this purpose.
I want to leave it to the province to make the selection.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
The selection may, I think, very well be left to an agreement between the provincial and the federal authorities. That phase of the question was very fully discussed at the interprovincial conference.
I was present during all the conferences, and not the slightest objection was-made by the premiers of the provinces to this method of procedure. They referred to the manner in which the administration of the Act respecting aid to agriculture had worked out, and intimated that they saw no reason why the same procedure should not hold good in the case of grants in aid of technical education. I do not, therefore, anticipate any difficulty in that regard.

I would suggest that agricultural education be included in this definition. The Government intends to encourage technical education, to develop our industries, and to promote the welfare of returned soldiers. I understand also that the Government have made arrangements with the various provinces under which returned soldiers will be induced to settle on the land. Agriculture is our basic industry. Broadly speaking, the two chief classes of the community are the workingmen and the farmers; why should the Gov-

eminent aid one class in the matter of education and not the other? Agriculture is a science, and in order that it may be carried on successfully it must be studied. In all countries large sums of money are spent for the development of agriculture and for agricultural education. I suggest that the minister add after the word " vocational " in the second line of paragraph (c) the word " agriculture ",

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has overlooked the fact that in 1913 an Act was passed in this House providing for grants for the very purpose which he mentions. Section 3 of that Act provided that for the purpose of aiding and advancing the farming industry by instruction in agriculture, and for the purposes authorized by the Act, a sum aggregating $10,000,000 should be distributed among the provinces in much the same way as is provided by this Bill.

The matter of technical education is one which comes within the purview of the various provinces. In vie* of the industrial development which has taken place, the provinces have been making efforts to promote special lines of education. Why should the Government not hand these sums to the provinces and let the provinces, without any string or agree. ments, continue the systems which they have developed? We must proceed on the assumption that the Provincial Governments are going to do their utmost, as they have done in the past, to promote technical education, and that they will use this money to the best advantage. There is a clause here which provides that in case of any disagreement the Minister of Labour shall be the sole and final judge. But there is a way of avoiding any disagreement. We are confident that the provinces will use this money for the purposes indicated in the Act; let us make the advances .to them and let them use the money for these purposes according to their particular requirements.
If we are doing this to assist the provinces in promoting technical education, to go on and develop further what they have already commenced to do, let us make conditions that they shall use the money for this specific purpose, hand over the money and let them distribute it as they please. A certain control must be exercised, but it ought not to go further than to say: We give you this money for technical educational purposes, and we trust you are going to carry out the purposes for which we give it to you. We ought to trust the provinces enough to permit them to administer the money without any specific agreement, without any surmise that they will not use it according to the intention, or even suspecting that a disagreement may arise requiring a court to decide it. I do not anticipate any disagreement, because I know there is enough laudable rivalry between the provinces as regards education that we may trust them to use the money to the best possible advantage.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: I can only repeat what I have already said, namely, that that phase of the question was very fully discussed at the conference. I was present at the conference, took part in the discussion, heard everything that was said, and I am quite within the mark when I state that at the conference not the slightest objection was raised along the line mentioned by the hon. member. The conference agreed that if grants of this kind were given, the Federal Government should retain the right to enter into agreements for the expenditure of that money just as they had done under the Agricultural Aid Act, and it was further stated freely by the provincial representatives that in the working out of that law 'no difficulty had been met at all, that everything was running along harmoniously, and that they expected the same would occur in the administration of this legislation. As a matter of fact, the question of arranging for some sort of inspection to see that this money was expended for the purposes mentioned in this Bill, was discussed, and the provinces agreed if the Federal Government thought that necessary, to allow federal inspectors to go into their institutions in order to see that the money was expended properly. I thoroughly agree in one sense with the viewpoint of the hon. member (Mr. Bureau), but we shall not reach that stage until we make direct subsidies to the provinces to a greater extent than they are now receiving in order that they may carry on their affairs as they see fit. Just so long as we must make special provision by federal acts, by special grants to the provinces, the expenditures of those moneys must be a matter of arrangement. Personally I would be only too glad if the time had arrived when an arrangement * could be entered into whereby the provinces would receive a larger sum in order that they might carry on their domestic affairs as they see fit; but we have not reached that stage yet, and it may be some time before it is reached.

I quite agree
with the minister that the best system would

be for the Dominion to advance the money to the provinces and to allow the provinces to use it in their best judgment for technical education or any other matter in the provinces. I pressed that view on the minister at the time when he introduced the resolution, advocating that he amend his Bill so as to adopt that principle. There are many cases in which the Federal Government is trying to tie up the Provincial Governments in regard to provincial expenditures. This is not the only one; I know other similar efforts are being made to control the policy of the provinces as regards questions of this kind. That is not a good policy. My hon. friend says that the time has not yet arrived. The time seems never to arrive with my hon. friend; it is always to-morrow that things are to be done. There cannot be a better time than the present to do this, because we are now embarking upon the course of assisting technical education. It will not be denied by my hon. friend that in every province a great deal of interest is being taken in this question, and splendid work is being done in certain provinces now in the prosecution of technical education. Surely, if this be the case, we can very well trust the provinces in the expenditure of the money. In the United States there is a similar system by which, I understand, money derived from public lands of the western States is used for purposes of technical education in various States. The State has to comply with certain regulations, to furnish certain equipment, before it can partake of the grant; but a condition of that kind would be -reasonable for my hon. friend to impose. The Act in the United States is called the Morell Act. This system has been in existence in the United States for a good many years, and I understand the Federal Government there does not exercise the, same control as my hon. friend purposes exercising over the provinces I see no good rea-_ son why this should be done, and I think the point is well taken, and I should like if my hon. friend would give it his consideration now and this money be given to the provinces without any string to it, without the Federal Government's exercising any control over the manner in which it is to be expended, except that it shall be expended for technical education and that the province shall do its share in providing certain funds. That would be a reasonable proposition; but when my hon. friend undertakes to lay down the kind of technical education a province shall teach, he is going a little too faT. The hon. mem-
ber for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) has pointed out that the interests of the several provinces differ very much, and it is by the province itself that that question can best be decided and not by the Federal Government.

I am glad this point has been raised as I intended to raise it myself. I view wilth a certain degree of apprehension these pieces of legislation which relate to matters coming under provincial jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: I think the hon. member will consider that this question is not entirely within provincial jurisdiction. If he followed the discussion which took place in this House two or three years ago on the motion of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), he will know that the general consensus of opinion was that the Federal Government had concurrent jurisdiction in this particular field of technical education, and I should like him to bear that in mind in his remarks.

The kind of education to be given and the manner of giving it are purely provincial matters. The Government could certainly help the various provinces by way of subsidies, but as the hon. members for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) and Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) have stated, no string should be attached to the grant given by the Federal Government. Formerly in this country many big battles were waged on this principle. The Government have tried to get around the difficulty in this way:
Instead of .taking away the rights of the provinces outright, they seem in some way to buy those rights by giving money to the provinces under certain conditions, which conditions, after all, involve the surrendering by the provinces of some of their rights and privileges. At the time of Confederation the provinces relinquished some of their rights to the Federal Parliament, and retained other rights. Now it is not fair for this Parliament to interfere in matters reserved exclusively for provincial jurisdiction, even by way of giving subsidy under certain conditions. My hon. friend says, and the Bill states, that there should be agreements between the minister and the different provinces before the grant is made. Now, if one of the provinces fails to reach an agreement with the minister, that province will not get anything, but the citizens of that province will be taxed to pay for education in another province which should be paid for altogether by the citizens of that second province. That is

not fair. If it can be done with regard to technical education it may be done with regard to anything else.
Take the question of national schools which was raised here the other day. I did not happen to be present when the matter was under discussion, but I think most hon. members will agree that that is a matter which does not come within the jurisdiction of this Parliament. The question of education is a very delicate question in this country. Suppose this Government does in the matter of national schools what it proposes to do in the matter of technical schools, and grants subsidies to the provinces provided those moneys, shall be spent on the establishment of national schools, would that be fair? Some of the provinces would refuse to accept the money. Would it be fair for this Parliament to ask the citizens of those provinces to pay for education in other provinces, when education is a matter of exclusive provincial concern?
I think the Government, should consider very seriously before taking away to such an extent the rights of the provinces, especially at a time when we are not blessed with so much money that we do not know where to spend it. At the present time there is a gap to be filled between our expenditure and our revenue, and we do not know where to get the money, and I submit that now is not the time to give away millions and millions of dollars either for highways or technical education or anything else which is a matter of exclusive provincial jurisdiction. If the country was in a state of great prosperity we could afford to be generous, but. in view of the financial condition I think we should wait a little before giving away this money especially in connection with a matter which is not under federal jurisdiction.

When the Minister of Immigration brought down the resolution upon which this Bill is based, he will remember, I called his attention to the fact that it might interfere with provincial autonomy. I suggested at the time that instead of the Federal Government launching upon a programme of housing, highways, and technical education, it would be wiser and more advantageous to the country at large simply to grant a subsidy and leave these matters to be worked out by the provinces. The provinces would be only too glad to encourage technical education. They have not been able to do much in the matter up to the present moment, especially the smaller provinces, because of lack of funds.
In New Brunswick, for instance, it is entirely due to lack of funds that in the matter of education we have not progressed like the provinces of Nova Scotia, Quebec and Ontario, which have much larger revenues. At the same time, during the last ten years, the expenditure of the province of New Brunswick on education is double and treble the amount we spent in former years. Ever since the admirable report of Dr. Robertson on technical education, six or seven years ago, we have been awaiting with anxiety the decision of the Government, to apportion that amount of $10,000,000 according to the very letter of his recommendations. That report did not say that there should be an agreement between the Federal Government and the provinces regarding the manner in which the money was to be spent. I was under the impression, from the minister's reply when the resolution was under discussion, that there would be no such provision as we find provided for an agreement between the Federal and Provincial Governments, but that the money would be given to the provinces to be spent as in their judgment seemed best to meet * the local needs. I trust the minister will consider the objections made by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House who have preceded me, and that every safeguard will be provided against any interference on the part of the Federal Government. The minister might say that provincial autonomy is well safeguarded in this Bill, but I trust that after he has heard our arguments he will accept the proposed amendment of my hon. friend from Kamouraska.

The province of Quebec would never have entered into Confederation unless guarantees had been given that education would be absolutely and exclusively within the competency of the Provincial Government. This is a Bill purporting to encourage technical education. Now, education, as the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) has said, is a matter of the greatest importance. The greatest and the most unfortunate conflicts we have had in Canada have arisen out of educational matters. It is needless for me to remind the House of the unfortunate conflicts which arose, for instance, in the province of New Brunswick at the beginning of the Confederation era, or of what happened in Manitoba, and in more recent years, in the province of Ontario. These conflicts on educational matters have retarded the union of the different races in Canada, and the less we have of them the better for all concerned.

This Bill, although it does not appear to be so, is in reality a very serious encroachment on provincial rights. The Bill provides that should there be any conflict between the Federal Government and the Pio-vincial Government the matter would be decided by the minister. The minister would therefore have the right to impose his views on a province in connection with an altogether provincial matter. Further, the Federal Government will have the right to appoint all officials in connection with the operation of this law, with the result that the minister may appoint a man to go into Ontario, Manitoba or British Columbia and in connection with their technical schools impose his decisions on the Provincial Government. That principle is a very unsound one and violates in a flagrant manner the agreement entered into by all the provinces in 1867, when it was agreed among the provinces that formed at that time the Canadian federation, that matters educational would be left altogether within the purview of the provinces without any interference from the Federal Government. If the Federal Government wishes, and has the means, to be generous, let it enable the provincial authorities to promote technical education. But as hon. members have already said, let these grants of money be without any string whatever. We do not wish to have educational conflicts in Canada, and if this Bill is passed as it is now, we shall have a direct intervention of the Federal Government in educational matters, which are a most delicate point in this country as the Committee knows. I do not think that a Bill such as this would promote the welfare of our country, but to the contrary. If the Federal Government wishes to make grants to the provinces, let it give the money to the Provincial Governments and leave it to them to decide what to do with it. If these loans or grants are to be merely a pretext for the Federal Government to take hold of educational matters in the provinces, so far as I am concerned I would rather not have a cent, and retain the liberty and freedom that we enjoy in our province in regard to education.

From my viewpoint as well as from that of the hon. member, it would be more satisfactory if the provinces were placed in possession of sufficient funds, through increased subsidies, to handle these enterprises themselves, because in a large degree they are provincial. Still, however, as a choice between letting technical education go by the board and receiving aid for such purposes under this Bill, I prefer to have

the grants. I am not prepared to take so strong a view as to say that we should not have them at all. If we could define technical education in such clear and distinct terms as would be beyond the possibility of debate, perhaps that would be a help. But in the absence of such a definition, which,
I fancy, would be difficult, I see some reasons in favour of the agreement which, I think, ought to commend themselves to my hon. friend from Three Rivers and those who agree with him. If there is to be no clear, distinct and indisputable definition of what constitutes technical education, then it is most desirable that there should be an agreement with each province to guard against any dispute. The machinery is to be largely provincial, and more than that, the province can only avail itself of a grant on the condition that it shall put up a large amount of money. It is therefore of vital importance that the province and the Dominion shall come to an understanding at the beginning. If there is no general definition of technical education, and I admit the difficulty, there are advantages in having an agreement with each province at the beginning, because you could then adapt your agreement'-although uniformity is desirable if possible-to the different forms of technical education which the provinces already have. Without such an agreement you may find yourself getting into trouble with the Provincial Governments. It seems to me that from that viewpoint there is much to be said in favour of having such an agreement. The hon. minister will recall that in the resolution stage of this matter, anticipating the possibility of some difference between the Dominion and the province, I suggested that perhaps by the time the Bill came before the House he might have some draft of what he proposed to ask the province to sign. I do not anticipate for a moment that any effort will be made to crowd out any particular province. Least of all do I fear, as my hon. friends from Quebec do, that any interference will be made with the recognized principle that the local governments control education. As regards technical education, it is worth remembering that this grant, although it is late in coming, is the outcome of a policy which the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier took up some years ago, when we appointed a technical education commission which made a tour of the world and gathered information, upon which they made a most valuable report. It is sometimes made a matter of complaint against the governments of a later day that

they pigeon-holed that report and did nothing. Well, the Government is doing something now, and I would rather have them do it in this way than do nothing at all. When the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier appointed that commission, headed by Professor Robertson and including a number of able men, we certainly created the impression that in some degree the matter was a Dominion one, and I look upon this movement as a belated endeavour on the part of the Government to carry out the intentions which tihe Liberal Government had in mind when they appointed that commission. There is, however, force in the criticism that the minister has too much individual power in this matter, and provision should be made that any report he makes under this Act should, at all events, be subject to approval by the Governor in Council.

I do not wish to be understood as objecting to a federal grant to the provinces for technical education. My objection is to the procedure and the mode in which the grant is to be made. It was never intended by the previous Administration that the grants to be made for technical education should be subject to certain terms or conditions or any specific agreement, or should be determined by special considerations to be laid down by the Federal Government.
I do not think they got as far as that.

No, but there was talk of it, and I for one certainly would not entertain for a moment the suggestion that any agreement should be made necessary that would in any way restrict the policies which have been established by the various provinces. There is a good deal in what the member for Kamouraska says. It is possible that some provinces may not take advantage of the scheme, owing perhaps to some condition imposed, and if no agreement could be reached between a province and the Federal Government it would be most unfair that that particular province should be called upon to pay any part of the subsidy that might be paid to other provinces. If the Federal authorities are in earnest about this matter and are really anxious to develop technical education, they should trust the provinces and rely upon their seeing that the money advanced shall be used to the best possible advantage. Why give rise to any suspicion as certain legislation has heretofore done? As my hon. friend from Kamouraska says, this
matter may be regarded as a bait for the provinces to enter into agreements to receive money for technical education purposes. He pointed out that if this principle extended to some other system of education and some province should refuse to enter into any agreement with the Federal Government, it would be unfair to tax that province. I do not believe that the minister need have any fear about the misuse of the money which may be granted to the provinces for technical education purposes.
The minister can put it in another way; he can say that no amount greater than the amount expended by the province shall be granted. Let the province be allowed to expend the money. If the minister is entirely satisfied that the money has been expended for the purpose for which it was intended, let the grant be paid. There can be no misunderstanding or dispute. Technical education may be different in different provinces, and it may cover various branches of industry and manufacture. Let the Federal Government determine that the amount to be granted shall be granted upon the basis of the population and the expenditure made by the province, and let the money be paid over without requiring them to enter into any agreement defining what form of technical education shall take in a certain province, and without having to pass a law with so many clauses as this. As far as the other danger which was pointed out by my hon. friend from Dorchester and my hon. friend from Kamouraska is concerned, I think, to use the expression that hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House used in 1911, it is the entering of the thin edge of the wedge, and it is an encrochment by the federal authorities on provincial rights in so far as education is concerned. I have enough confidence in any province to say: Here is the money for technical education; take it and use it for that purpose. If it is not used for that purpose the fact will be easily ascertained, and under those circumstances cut off the grant next year and let the province be deprived of the money that they would have otherwise have got for that special purpose. I do not see that any good reason has been given by the minister for this restriction and agreement. He says that at the conference of the premiers the matter was discussed and that they were all agreed. They could not do otherwise. We have a French saying, "A cheval donne on ne regarde pas a la bride." I do not know how it could be translated, but the meaning is that when some one makes you a present

of a horse you do not examine the harness in detail.
You do not look a gift horse in the mouth.

You do not look a gift horse in the mouth, my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) says, but in this ease you do not have to, because it would cost you too much. We do not have to adopt the conclusion that members may draw, but we have to take into consideration the impression that this measure will create upon the minds of the outside public and the fears that may be created. We do not know what will happen. Things change so fast these days that we must be prepared for almost anything happening, and we must try to prevent anything happening that may give rise to the idea that something is being done which will curtail the rights of the provinces. It would be very easy for the minister to say: This Government will give so much money; this money shall be proportioned according to the population; it shall be payable in so many years, and the province which desires to have the benefit of the money shall spend so much for technical education purposes. I think that would cover the ground and it would do away with any idea that this is the beginning of an encroachment upon provincial rights. Of course, it was hard for the provincial ministers to discuss the question of provincial rights at the time of the conference. They did not know what the provisions of the Bill were to be. The details were not enumerated. These men were prepared to say that they would use the money for the purposes of technical education, but they wanted the Government to take their word for it. The Federal Government says that it has the jurisdiction and that it ought to be the final judge as to the proper use to be made of this money, but it ought to have enough confidence in the other people to take it for granted that the money will be used for the purpose for which it is appropriated and for that purpose alone. Rivalry in education is noble and laudable. There has been sufficient industrial development, and there have been enough sacrifices made by the provinces to establish industrial schools and provide technical education, that the Government should not be afraid, or feel the least suspicion, that this money will be diverted from the purpose. for which it is granted. This grant ought to be made nobly and grandly and you should say to the provinces: " Here is the money; use it to pro-
LMr. Bureau.]
mote technical education." I think that should be sufficient.
Mr. MANION. I thoroughly agree with the granting of aid by this Parliament for educational purposes, particularly technical education, but at the same time I feel that there is a good deal to be said for the arguments of the last speakers, the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). With many of the points made by the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) I entirely agree, but I do not agree with one argument he put up and that was that at this time when money is so much needed in this country we should perhaps consider not making this grant for educational purposes. Education is perhaps the most important question to be considered next to that of the health of our people, and I do not think that because of this war we should permit ourselves to be stampeded into withholding money that is so much needed for technical education. The point I would like to make regarding the importance of education is that if you look over the commercial history of the world for the fifteen or, twenty years previous to the war you will find that the United States and Germany were rapidly gaining upon England commercially and the reason was that Germany and the United States stood very high with regard to their systems and types of technical education. The United States spent vast amounts of money on their educational system, including technical education, and I took the opportunity the other day of putting down some figures from a pamphlet that I read that I thought would be interesting to this House in regard to the amount of money spent by the United States on education, including technical education. The sums are stupendous as will be shown by the following statement:
