I mention the contributions of Messrs. Rockefeller and Carnegie because they might possibly give a certain amount of inspiration to some of the gentlemen in our country who have made vast amounts of money out of the war. With regard to the points mentioned by the hon. member for Three Rivers, the hon. member for Kamour-

aska and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's I believe many of them are well taken. There is no question which has been thought of so jealously by the provinces as that of education. I do not believe there is any real basis for the fear in some of the provinces that this may be the entering of the thin end of the wedge of interference with the present system of education in those provinces, but I think we have enough causes for misunderstanding in this country-and I believe they are misunderstandings and ont intentional injuries to any province-to make us careful and avoid the possibility of giving cause for any fresh misunderstanding at the present time. For example, I notice that one paragraph in the Bill says:
The minister shall toe the sole judge of all questions and differences that may arise under this Act or under any agreement made in pursuance of this Act.
In another paragraph it is provided that if the minister is not satisfied that the money was to be used to his satisfaction by a certain province he may refuse to grant it. My own personal opinion is that that is too much power to put in the hands of any minister. I do not for one moment believe that any of the present Federal ministers would think of using that power wrongly; but in my opinion, too great a power should not be placed in the hands of any one minister. I think if the Government decides upon such a paragraph as that remaining in the Bill the suggestion of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) that the power be vested in the Governor in .Council rather than in a single member of the Cabinet would be a far better provision. At the same time I believe that the point made by another hon. gentleman is a good one, to this effect-that the money should be given to the province with the distinct understanding that it be spent on technical education. If it is not so spent the grant should be withheld the following year. I believe the Government would be well advised in any question of this kind to avoid in the case of any particular section of *Canada any cause for misunderstanding. I wish to say positively that I believe that if any unpleasantness arose it would be due only to a misunderstanding, because I do not mean to insinuate for a moment that any member of the Government would wrongly use the power granted under this legislation. I repeat, however, that we should not give too much power to any minister and the substitution of Governor in Council in the questionable clause might he better.

If I apprehend the matter correctly the same principle is involved in this legislation as was embodied in the law by which special grants are made by the Dominion Government for the purpose of promoting agriculture in the several provinces, and also in the Bill still before the House providing for Dominion assistance towards the construction of highways. Under the present Bill the provinces will contribute money equally with the Dominion, and that before any agreement can be entered into between the Federal and provincial authorities. It may be said, why not give this money as additional subsidy to the provinces and not have any limitations such as are here provided. As I understand the proposition it is experimental in this way: The grant is limited to a period of ten years in the first place, doubtless with the idea of seeing how the matter will work out. At the end of that time it may be possible to provide new conditions and new arrangements, but in the meantime it does seem reasonable that while the federal and provincial authorities are equally to make grants there should be an agreement entered into as to what the nature of technical education should be. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bureau) does not seem to entertain any distrust of the Provincial Governments; he is fully convinced they will carry out their part of the agreement, he is willing to trust them through thick and thin. Why should he not have equal confidence in the Federal Government or in the federal minister who may be empowered to enter into this arrangement? His confidence seems to be a little one-sided. The spirit of generosity and confidence which he expresses ought to be extended to the Dominion Government as well.- Of course, if a Provincial Government is unwilling to enter into an agreement with the Federal Government, I suppose there is no obligation on their part to accept the money; they can appropriate money from their own revenues for the purpose if they choose. In any case the arrangement is only tentative, as I understand, and would apply only to a period of ten years in order that it shall be seen how the arrangement will work out. That is the way the situation presents itself to me. To my mind, the proposed legislation does not offer any insuperable difficulty. As to the suggestion of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) that the Governor in Council might be a court of appeal, so to speak, in case any dispute should arise between the federal authorities and a Provincial Government, that might be well, but

the proposition in its present form does not seem to me to afford any reason for objecting to an agreement with any Provincial Government, or any one really desirous that the experiment of introducing and advancing technical education in his province should be tried.

I am sure we * are all
very glad that the Federal Government is making some provision for aiding technical education in the provinces, although I suppose there will be differences of opinion as to ways and means. I think that if we study the Bill on its face and do not attempt to read into it what is not to be found there, there is practically very little to cause any alarm. As the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) has pointed out, this is really the second step on the part of this House to carry out in part the recommendations of the Robertson Commission. I am not familiar with the Act which has made possible certain work along the lines of agriculture, but so far as I can learn the money granted to the provinces desirous' of using it, on the advice of the Commissioner of Agriculture, has so far been wisely expended and received and used by the provinces in such a way as to commend their action to 'the Department of Agriculture here. My impression is that the Minister of Agriculture from year to year has had a good deal to say, in consultation with his Commissioner, in connection with the expenditure of that money, amounting to nearly a million dollars a year. I do not see why there should be any objection to conditions being insisted upon such as are provided in this legislation-in fact, this Parliament should not vote large sums of money to the provinces for this, or any similar purpose, without the imposition of some conditions, and especially where the provincial governments have a great deal to say in making the necessary agreements and adjustments so far as details are concerned. I think we know that the representatives mainly called upon to act in the several provinces will be the Minister of Agriculture and the Premier. These two men in most of the provinces would have the most to say. I think one of the things we must bear in mind in making a grant for technical education to a province is whether the money shall be spent on capital account, for example, or in connection with current expenditure. As one who comes from a western province where our equipment and our buildings as well are still in the pioneer stage, I do noit think for one moment that we in this House could vote
.
for a blanket grant to the province of Manitoba for technical education with the understanding that the Provincial Minister of Education could decide perhaps, that, during the first year all of that money was to be spent for buildings and equipment in the city of Brandon.
I think it would be a misuse of funds, Mr. Chairman. Therefore, I favour the laying down of fair and Reasonable conditions under which these moneys shall be advanced. If any wise multi-millionaire should at any time-I hope it may be in the near future-establish an educational fund and make possible the expenditure of a million dollars a year on some particular kind of technical education, that fund could best be administered by a group of trustees, and any province or municipality accepting moneys out of that fund would undoubtedly have to agree to certain conditions; otherwise the trustees could not provide for the distribution oi the moneys. I realize that the analogy is not perfect; that, as the member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) has said, one of the provinces may be unwilling to accept the conditions, and, having in a sense contributed a part of the $10,000,000 to the Dominion Treasury, would no't get back its share of it for the purposes of technical education. But I believe there would be very little danger of that; I do not think we need be afraid of the result of laying down reasonable conditions. We ought to trust each other a little; the federal authorities should repose some confidence in provincial departments, and vice versa.
One word with regard to a remark made by my hon. friend (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) in connection with the experience of the United States government in this matter. Leading -authorities in technical education in the United States have felt for some years that the Federal Government made grave mistakes shortly after the conclusion of the civil war, during the early part of their reconstruction period, by making blanket grants for agriculture. They had no way of conserving the investments that they made -and it is felt by those who have studied these investments that they w7ere very largely wasted. With regard ito the more recent grants in 'aid of technical education imade by the United States government there is a feeling that there must be a measure of fair control; there must be a few simple conditions if the investments made are to be conserved in the interest of the nation -as a whole. I support the Bill as it stands.

Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that he would not trust the Government of Manitoba with the expenditure of money for buildings in Brandon unless control was exercised over the expenditure by the federal authorities?

No, I do not say that. I said that I would not want to see money granted to Manitoba spent in any one year on buildings and equipment in the city of Brandon.	.
Mr, BUREAU: Probably they would not do it.
But they might, if you granted it without laying down any conditions.
If we are to proceed on supposition and hypotheses, then I say that the Federal Government might do worse.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I had the privilege of introducing into this House the Agricultural Instruction Act, and had something to do with its subsequent operation. Although it is not precisely the same as this-
There is all the difference in the world. You have a Department of Agriculture here, and there is concurrent jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I would not say that there is all the difference in the world, though I admit that the two Acts are not exactly on the same footing. But there is a sufficient analogy to enable a good many of the same arguments to apply to both cases. It is one of the first principles that when Parliament votes, money it must exercise a certain amount of control in connection with the expenditure of that money. In fact, it was strongly urged, not only from our side of the House but also by hon. gentlemen opposite when the Agricultural Instruction Act was introduced, that there was not sufficient federal control over the expenditure of the money which was being advanced. I did not take that view, because it seemed to me that the scheme as it worked out in the Act would develop on lines that would be thoroughly satisfactory to the federal and to the provincial authorities. Under that Act a certain sum was granted, which this year amounts to $1,100,000, for distribution among the various provinces. The conditions under which the expenditures were to be made were laid down broadly in the Bill itself, and agreements were entered into between myself as Minister of Agriculture and the Min241
isters of Agriculture of the different provinces in which, after a general discussion of the whole subject had been had, the class of work which would rightly come under the provisions of the Act was laid down. Occasionally there would be disputes on the question whether such-and-such a line of activity did come within the scope of the Bill, but these differences were finally adjusted amicably, and I am quite sure that the fact that the discussions were held served a good purpose and led to unity of action. It was much better to do this than simply to hand over a sum of money to the provinces which they might expend as they saw fit, and then find out afterwards whether or not the money was properly spent. The member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) suggested that this money be handed over to the provinces to be spent by them on technical education as they might themselves determine, and if there were any disputes afterwards we might withhold the money at another time. His contention was that we should trust the provinces. But I am absolutely sure that in any agreement that is made the air will be cleared and satisfactory arrangements will be come to. As a matter of fact, in connection with the Agricultural Instruction Act, once we got the thing working on lines that were mutually agreeable, the programme for this educational work was really laid down by the provinces themselves; the federal minister simply made suggestions as to whether the expenditure of moneys on a particular line of activity was in accordance with the terms of the Act or not, and so on. That procedure led to greater continuity, and there was no difficulty at all. Nor do I apprehend any difficulty in connection with this Act. The minister representing the province concerned will, I have no doubt, outline the conditions in that province, state what work they are doing and what schemes they are carrying out, and I am sure that any agreement arrived at will meet the views of both Governments and still preserve a rightful measure of control or supervision by this Parliament over the expenditure. I would expect such a procedure to simplify the situation rather than complicate it, as my hon. friend suggests. As to. handing the money over to the provinces with the idea that they, might spend it as they wish, we must remember that provincial governments change from time to time and that ministers change; you may have great discretion in one case and great indiscretion in another. I think it will

lead to far less confusion, to greater unity of purpose, and to continuity of effort if the provinces and the Federal Government agree from year to year upon what form the expenditure shall take. I feel sure that there will he no trouble at all in that connection.
Mr. OAiLDEE:	The point at issue is
quite clear, that is, whether or not the Federal Government should retain any measure of supervision over these expenditures, or whether some money should be given directly to the provinces to be expended by them as they see fit for purposes of technical education. I do not see that I can add anything to the argument, as the whole case has been placed before the committee. The Government, after considering the whole proposition have come to the conclusion that the wisest thing to do, under all the circumstances, is to carry out the idea as embodied in the Bill, and very largely for the reasons explained by the Secretary of State (Mr. Burrell) and for those given by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Whidden). In the United States the federal system is very much as it is here. Education is a State right. The Federal Government does not interfere with education in the various States. Nevertheless, during the past ten or fifteen years it has made many provisions of a similar character for aiding in agricultural, vocational and technical education, and in every one of those instances under the various laws, the United Stales Federal Government has retained a measure of control and supervision. Under their last law, passed in 1817 called, I think, the Smith-Hughes law, provision is made for very liberal machinery for the purpose of co-operating with the States, and, I think, for a very definite, specific and useful purpose, the purpose mentioned by the Secretary of State (Mr. Burrell). That is, if we can succeed in getting all the provinces in Canada to endeavour to work as far as possible along well-defined modern lines to secure the one result for the whole of Canada, instead of each province working as a separate unit, in the end we shall secure better results. As a result of the many conferences that were held between the representative of the Department of Agriculture, Mr. James, who is looked upon as one of the best agriculturists in Canada, and the heads and chief officials of the Provincial Departments of Agriculture for the purpose of considering what was best to be done in the interest of agricultural education in each province, I have no hesitation in saying that the $1,100,000 that has
I Mr. Burrell.]
been expended up to date is being far more wisely expended than if the matter had been left entirely to the discretion of the Provincial Governments. Last fall we had the	largest interpfovincial	conferenceever	held in	Canada, comprising	allthe	premiers	and from	three	tofive	ministers	from some	of	the
provinces, and we had a very interesting and important conference. This matter was very fully discussed, and I do not think the representatives who were present hesitated to speak their minds. They spoke their minds on other subjects very freely, and during the whole discussion, if I remember aright-and .1 think I do-not the slightest objection was raised by any representative at that conference to the conditions underlying the aid given under the Agricultural Aid Act.
(Mr. BUREAU: That is different.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
That is quite true, but
when we were discussing the question of providing a system of grants for technical education, time and again reference was made to the manner in which the matter had been worked out as regards the Agricultural Aid Act, and there was not the slightest indication upon the part of any representative at that gathering that any difficulty at all was anticipated. The Secretary of State has put his finger on a principle we cannot overlook. Where the Federal Government is making a grant for a specific purpose, we have a right to retain a measure of control in order to see that that money is expended for that purpose. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's referred to this agreement being made by the Minister of Labour. He will find, however, that under clause 6 every such agreement must be submitted to Council and approved by the Governor in Council.
There is a later clause which says that in the event of a dispute the minister shall be the sole judge. It was to that clause I referred.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: Yes. Individual agreements with the provinces must all be approved by the Governor in Council. As regards the Minister of Labour being the sole'judge in case any dispute arises under an agreement, I am quite prepared to meet the wishes of the Committee. I can see where there may be an objection to that provision, and we are quite willing to frame the clause so as to meet the objection which has been brought to our attention.

The minister seems to want to get out of this by referring to agriculture, and the Secretary of State seems to put the two classes on a similar basis. There is all the difference in the world between the two classes. In the Department of Agriculture at Ottawa, the work is, I understand, mainly along experimental lines, and it has all the equipment necessary to assist the provinces and to work in cooperation with them. But in this case the Government, in making a grant, wants to have a string on the end of its generosity so that the grant may be pulled back at pleasure, and this in a matter in which the Federal Government has no jurisdiction and which is entirely and exclusively within the jurisdiction of the provinces; and I may say that this is liable to cause suspicion to the outside world. The two cases are not on a par at all. If the Government wants to make a grant-this is not experimental work, we want to educate our children in certain trades and sciences-it is very easy for the minister to say: These are the conditions we are to impose upon those who want to benefit by the grant; you shall use the money for building technical schools or for salaries for technical instructors; those who want to benefit will come.and take it; everybody is on the same footing; Parliament will support that, and Parliament will discuss and determine the conditions under which it is willing to vote the money and to give it to the provinces for such special purposes.
The Secretary of State says that Provincial Governments may change, and that a different Minister of Education in a province may not be up to the standard of his predecessor, or he may be unwilling. That argument works both ways. This Government may change, and if you are going to distrust the provinces there is no reason why you should not distrust this Government. If you are going to make a grant, do not ask the provinces to come on their knees and sign all sorts of agreement. Let Parliament that votes the money determine on what conditions the money shall be given to the provinces. Let the whole world know what the conditions are. Let the statutes define what shall constitute technical education, and let Parliament declare under what conditions the grant shall be given, and under what conditions it shall be refused. There is no danger, however, of any province refusing the money; at least, I hope not. Now I do not want my words to be distorted; I do not want to be understood as being opposed
2412:
to this grant. It is not the grant we are considering, but simply a question of ways and means. I say that if we are to vote the money we should determine the conditions under which it shall be given, and': let everybody know the conditions. There is another clause in this Bill-I may not-be in order in referring to it now, but we have to take the Bill as a whole-which' says that the grant shall not be used for extinguishing any indebtedness or liability incurred before the 1st of July of this year.
I think that is hardly fair. A province, for instance, which has taken the lead in educational matters may have bought sites and put up buildings. Is that province to be penalized because it has gone ahead of the others?
Let it keep ahead.

Why should it not be allowed to use the grant for extinguishing the indebtedness incurred in buying the site and erecting the building? Why should it be penalized for what it has done? A province that makes a contract for the erection of a building or the purchase of a site 011 2nd July can use the grant for extinguishing that indebtedness, whereas the province that made its contract on 29th June cannot do so; yet each province may have expended the same amount of money.
I think that provision should not be in the Bill. That is why I say, let us determine here in this Parliament the conditions under which the provinces shall be entitled to receive the money, and then let the Government decide before making the grant whether the provinces come within the four corners of the law. If they do, let them get the grant and dispose of it for technical educational purposes as in their judgment seems best.

The Secretary of State, an ex-Minister of Agriculture, (Mr. Burrell) has told us of what took place in the matter of agricultural education as between the Federal Government and the provinces. iNow we cannot compare agricultural education with other educational work. There is a special clause in the British North America Act providing for cooperation between the1 Department of Agriculture in the Federal Government and the provinces in matters of agriculture, but another clause makes it imperative that edur cation shall be left solely to the provinces, and without that clause Confederation would not have been accomplished. It is one of the most vital clauses in the British North America Act, and the one perhaps most conducive to the happiness of the

people. My hon. friend when Minister of Agriculture was perfectly within his rights -in trying to bring about co-operation between the provinces and the Federal Government in matters pertaining to the development of agriculture, but I claim that the Minister of Immigration and Colonization is not in the name position, and therefore we must safeguard provincial rights 1 which are here endangered. I want the money to be given to the provinces fer technical education. We all know that *every province is anxious to have technical education, and I believe they are all willing and anxious to co-operate in every possible way for its development. The minister need have no fear that the money will not be spent for that purpose. I say that the provinces should be allowed to decide in what way the money shall be spent. It m^y be that in some provinces where technical education is not so far advanced as in others, in New Brunswick, for instance, for the first year or so perhaps the teachers of the primary schools may be entrusted with the duty of imparting technical education. At all events, all that the Federal Government is interested in is that the money is spent for the purposes of technical education. If the grant was made to the provinces and they were left to decide how it should be spent, without any conditions being imposed by this Government, there would be no encroachment upon provincial rights, which are always regarded jealously by the provinces. I trust, therefore, that the minister will be satisfied with a provision that will enable the provinces that receive the grant to spend it for the purposes of technical education according to their best judgment.

I realize that to ' oppose the granting of any money to the provinces is not a very popular thing, but as far as I am concerned, I would oppose the granting of this money if by accepting it the provinces have to relinquish any of their provincial rights. I think the mere fact that the ministers are citing the grant for aid to agriculture as a precedent, shows how dangerous this legislation is. The two things cannot be compared, because agriculture comes under federal jurisdiction as well as under provincial jurisdiction; but that is not the case with regard to education. The British North America Act explicitly provides that education comes exclusively-the word " exclusively " is used in the Act-under provincial jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
If you want to laboui that point you can apply precisely the same
CMr. Turgeon.]
argument in the case of the Agricultural Instruction Act-not the Act for aid to agriculture; that was the first Bill, passed in 1912-because the work we were carrying on under that Act was educational work. This Government was not establishing, and never has established, agricultural colleges or carried on educational work, but the money was voted specifically for educational purposes.
Experimental farms are educational work.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: If you are going to argue that, then every form of governmental activity is, in some sense, educational. The specific educational work, as far as it applied to agriculture, was done under this Agricultural Instruction Act and was done by the provinces. I am sure there is no invasion of provincial jurisdiction because practically they would mutually agree. My hon. friend is rather anticipating a bogey that does not really exist.
This shows more clearly the danger of establishing such precedents. This Government started by giving agricultural aid to the provinces. Next came educational help with regard to agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: For which they were very glad.

Now it is used as a precedent to give help to technical education, this Government keeping control of the manner in which the education shall be carried on. Other matters will arise, and the legislation of to-night will be used as a precedent for new legislation. The first precedent is agricultural education, and the second is technical education. As I said at an early stage of the proceedings, nothing will prevent a government, with such precedents, to give subsidies to provinces which will be willing to establish national schools within their borders. This is a dangerous procedure. This Government is gradually encroaching on the provincial area and it has done so in many matters. Take the question of the Department of Health which has been created this year. I have read in Hansard of many years ago a debate when a resolution to create such a department was proposed in the House of Commons at a time when Sir John A. Macdonald was Prime Minister. Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir Charles Tupper and other leading statesmen of that time stated emphatically that under the British North America Act this

Government conld not establish a Department of Health. This year, of course, with all the precedents which the minister has adduced, a Department of Health has been created. The Government have given subsidies to the provinces for agricultural education, keeping control on that education. They want to give subsidies for technical education with a string attached, keeping control on a purely provincial matter; and they will do it in other cases on the strength of the precedent which we aTe creating to-night. The Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) says there has been an inter-provincial conference at which no one objected. I would submit that the proceedings of provincial conferences should be made public. The atmosphere of the 20th century is not conducive to secret proceedings. If the great diplomats of the world have to make their proceedings public, our own diplomats in Canada, the ministers of the Federal Government and of the various provinces, ought to make their proceedings absolutely public too. But even if the minister agreed to that, I submit, the Bill was not prepared at that time, and I would not be surprised to learn that all the conditions which I read in the various sections of the Bill were not submitted to the provincial ministers at that time. However, even if they were submitted and the provincial ministers agreed to the legislation, that would not relieve me of my responsibility, as a member of the Canadian House of Commons, of the duty to uphold the constitution of Canada so far as provincial jurisdiction is concerned. I am in earnest in the objections I have raised against this particular Bill. I want to tell my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) that I have not said I am opposed to technical education. I only said that this particular year is not a propitious year to give the money of this country to the provinces for works which are of a provincial character. The provinces are in a better position financially than this Government at the present time. I know some provinces which are in a pretty safe condition financially and are able to undertake works which come under their jurisdiction. Here, at this time, we do not know where to get money. I think expenditures which are of a purely provincial character should be borne by the provinces this year. When the country is more prosperous it will be time to consider the giving of help to the provinces by this Government. But, even then, I think this grant should be given freely to the provinces without any string attached to it. The provinces should be
free to expend the money for the purposes stipulated, and there should be no control by the Federal Government of questions that are purely provincial.

The essential fact that has been overlooked, that Parliament, which is responsible for collecting the money, must of necessity be responsible for the expending of it, and that when this Government votes a grant to any province for any purpose it must necessarily see that the money is spent for the purpose intended.
I cannot see how this could be done if the grant were not accompanied by some regulation. I agree with the statement of the member for Shelburne and Queen's on a former occasion that most of these objections generally disappear when accompanied by a large grant of money. I think the objections which have been raised to-night will not materialize to any great extent, and if they did I could not see the force of them. The difficulty ought to be overcome. It would be most unfortunate if a Bill of this kind, which holds out such great possibilities for Canada-and no doubt this matter is long overdue, for Canada has been living on the brains of the world to a great extent in industrial lines for a great many years- could not be taken advantage of by every province. As the hon. member for Three Rivers said, the provisions could be fought out and incorporated in the Bill. I am quite convinced that the Government must control the money and see that it is used for the purpose for which it is given. And it is necessary to see that the idea conveyed in the definition of technical education as given here is carried out by the provinces. As I said on a former occasion, it should also be seen to that the money is distributed to different parts of a province because education should be universal. The tendency in the past in all provinces has been to centre technical education in the cities and large towns, and even small cities have not benefited. That is one thing which should be guarded against in this Bill. Altogether, I think, the minister must of necessity accompany the grant with certain regulations.

The hon. member says
that expenditure of the money given by the Federal Government should be controlled by the Government. The argument at first appears to be a strong one, but in the relations between the Federal Government and the Provincial Governments large sums of money have been given by this Government, which has absolutely no right to supervise their expenditure. For

instance, the provincial subsidies given by the Federal Government every year amount to large sums. That money is given and it has never entered the mind of any minister of the Federal Cabinet to claim the right to ask an accounting of these moneys from the Provincial Governments.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: That is given under the terms of Confederation which is a very different situation.

But the reason for granting this in no way changes the system under which moneys have been given by the Federal Government to the Provincial Governments without the Federal Government retaining control or supervision thereof. If that can happen in connection with the payment of a subsidy I do not see why the same thing should not happen in connection with this Bill. The Secretary of State has made a comparison between his own Bill passed a few years ago and the Bill that is now being examined by the committee. I have under my hand the statutes of 1913 containing that Act. Without laying any stress on the argument put forward by my hon. friend from Kamou-raska that there is a wide difference between agriculture and technical education, I must say that there is a wide difference between the two Bills themselves. Section 2, paragraph (c) gives a definition of technical education so general and elastic that all kinds of things may be included in the interpretation of the words "technical education." The Bill regarding agriculture contains no such provision. Why should we, in this new Bill, provide that the Federal Government shall exact an agreement from the Provincial Governments and shall define education, technical or vocational, when no such requirement was made in regard to the grant for agricultural education? We find, as was pointed out by my hon. friend from Kamouraska, that the Bill passed in 1913 is being used as a precedent by the Minister of Immigration and Colonization. He says that after having passed a Bill as regards agriculture we are passing a similar Bill as regards technical education. But that Bill did not contain the definition that this Bill contains, and that is where the danger lies. We do not want in our province any federal interference with educational matters. We have had enough trouble in the past, we do not want to have any more trouble now. Our province, as regards technical education, has done wonders. The minister knows what Quebec has done. We have technical schools in Montreal, Quebec, Shawinigan,

Three Rivers and Sherbrooke. There is one being built in the city of Hull. I repeat, the province of Quebec has done wonders as regards technical education. We have never needed help from the Federal Government. Naturally, as business men our Government will certainly not refuse any help if it is being offered, but the Provincial Government and members from our province will not be willing to give away our privileges as regards education for any amount of money. If the Government wish to help us, we will not refuse the offer oi $100,000, or $200,000 or perhaps $500,000, but let not the Minister of Immigration or any other minister attempt to interfere with educational matters in our province. We do not admit the principle because it is a principle altogether opposed to the British North America Act and also to our privileges and interests.
Let the Bill concerning technical education be the same as the Bill concerning agricultural education. We will not take any, or as strong, objection as we have to the present Bill. But there is also a new clause and every one of these fiew clauses is an encroachment upon our present privileges. The Bill shows the tendency of the Federal Government to interfere with and encroach upon provincial rights. What is the reason? The reason is very obvious. Confederation was accepted at the time only as a compromise between certain portions of this country. We know that. Lots of people in this country, instead of having a confederation as we have it now, would have preferred a legislative union. That has been the aim of a great many people. The aspiration of those people has not died with them. They have their successors in politics; they have had their heirs. Of course, it is impossible to-day for any man, or any Provincial Government to come out and say directly: We want to abolish the present system; we want to have only one government, a central government sitting in Ottawa and governing this country. Any man who would propose such a system would have practically no hearing in any of the provinces. But the Government is clever. The Government is taking an indirect route to attain that object. It is giving money to the provinces in different forms and interfering with provincial matters in different ways. What will be the result? Very soon the Provincial Governments will have such liabilities towards the Federal Government that they will become the mere tools and instruments of the Federal Government, they will disappear and instead of having in Canada the beautiful

political machine invented by Sir John Macdonald, Sir George Etienne Cartier and many others, that system will be destroyed and we will have a central government. We are not in favour of a central government. We are in favour of the present state of affairs and in order to safeguard our privileges we insist that there shall be no encroachment. Compare the Bill referred to by the Secretary of State, which is chapter 6, 3 and 4 George V with this Bill. There are no clauses in that Act such as we find in the Bill. There is no provision that the minister shall be the sole judge in case of disagreement. Yet the minister comes with this Bill and says that his only aim and object is to help technical education in the provinces. Although he is giving money to the provinces, if he wishes to restrict their privileges we wrill not accept the Bill. We think the Bill may be interpreted in such a way as to enable the minister to interfere with our privileges. Therefore, we are against the Bill and no matter if we do lose the money, we would rather do so than give up any of our existing privileges.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: During the course of his remarks the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat made the statement that if this Bill providing for grants to technical education were practically on all fours with the Bill providing for agricultural education he would have no objection to it.
Not so many objections, I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
If I remember the hon.
gentleman's remarks correctly, he said he would have no objection.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: A portion of his song was that this Bill was materially different from the other Bills.

What does the minister
mean by " song " in this House?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
It has an ordinary meaning that I think everybody understands. I must ask the Committee at this stage to allow me a few minutes and I think after I close we may as well report progress and rise. But before the House adjourns tonight, I would like to make the members ' of the Committee acquainted with what the real provisions of the Agricultural Aid Act are. This Act, which was passed in 1913, was originally called the Agricultural Instruction Act, and its preamble reads as follows:
Whereas it is desirable that encouragement be given to agriculture in all the provinces of
Canada, and whereas great and permanent benefit will result to education, instruction and demonstration carried on along lines well devised and of a continuous nature



and so on. The third section of the
Bill reads as follows:
For the purpose of aiding and advancing the farming industry-
By what?
-by instruction in agriculture.
Would the minister be fair? I based my comparison mostly on section 1. Also, I would not like the minister to skip section 2 of the Agricultural Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will wait, I am coming to his main contention. His contention is that there is no definit'on in this Act of agricultural instruction.
The same as in this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
Exactly, the same as in this Bill, and the hon. gentleman takes exception because in section 2 of the Bill that is now being discussed there is provision for an agreement between the provinces and the Federal Government as to the manner in which these moneys shall be expended. Well, I do not understand the hon. gentleman at all. Just another moment, and I- am through. If the Committee will refer to section 5 of the Agricultural Instruction Act it will be found to contain this provision:
The payments hereinbefore authorized shall, as to each province, be conditional upon agreement between the minister and the Government of the province as to the terms, conditions, and purposes, within the meaning of this Act, upon and for which the payments are to he made and applied, and such agreement shall be subject to the approval of the Governor in Council.
That does not define " instruction,"

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: The two Bills are practically on all fours.
It does not define " instruction."

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: Neither is " technical instruction " defined
Certainly, it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: One of the objections made to the Bill by an hon. gentleman opposite is that as such instruction is not defined the Bill would be the better for it. Well, " agricultural instruction " as used in the other Act is not defined either.
Not defined at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
Now, section 7 of the Agricultural Instruction Act reads as follows:

The Governor In Council may make such regulations as are deemed advisable for giving effect to the objects and purposes of this Act, and, notwithstanding anything in this Act, the minister, with the approval of the Governor in Council and with the consent of the Lieutenant Governor in Council of any province and upon such terms and conditions as are prescribed by the Governor in Council, may expend in any such province in any year the whole or any part*, of the grant provided for such province under this Act for the purposes set forth in the preamble of this Act.
In other words, in the Agricultural Instruction Act there is the fullest provision made for the entering into of an agreement between the provinces and the Federal Government for the purpose of expending the grants provided for in any form of agricultural instruction that may be agreed upon between the provinces and the federal authorities, and that is exactly the provision in the present Bill. I can quite understand the argument that is advanced, that technical education is not exactly on the same basis as agricultural education, but that there is a wide difference between the provisions of the Agricultural Instruction Act and the provisions of this Bill, I cannot see at all.
Between the subject matters as stated.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: That is an entirely different thing. The view I have stated is the one that is taken by the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat.
What about section 6?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
